Mr., T. G. RODDICK (Montreal, St. Antoine) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 11) to provide for the establishment of a medical council in Canada. He said : Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up the time of the House at this stage with any lengthy remarks, but I would simply like your permission to say, Sir, that since I had the opportunity about a year ago in this House, of explaining this measure fully, I have met representatives of the medical profession from every province in the Dominion of Canada, at a convention held in the city of Winnipeg in August last at which this measure was endorsed in its entirety with one or two exceptions or amendments, notably an alteration in the proposed composition of the council. The council, will, under the present draft bill, be somewhat changed in its method of election ; that is to say, that instead of three representatives from each province, as was originally intended, the representation shall now be based oil the number of medical men in each province, making for the larger provinces a very considerable increase. Another change which was decided upon was to have the ten universities of Canada represented on this council. With the exception of these there have been no alterations in the original Bill as presented to this House at the last session of parliament. I have reason to believe that the medical men in this House, of whom there are fourteen or fifteen, are almost unanimous, if not unanimous, in their endorsation of this measure, and I hope they will join me in the request which I intend making on the second reading of this Bill, that the right hon. leader of the government shall cousent to the appointment of a com-

mitte, which shall be composed chiefly of the medical men of the House with one or two legal gentlemen, who shall have an opportunity of studying the measure and of hearing any delegates who may come from the various provinces in order to suggest changes or amendments in It. I have been anxious that the profession should thoroughly understand the measure, and now I am exceedingly anxious that the medical men in this House and my hon. friends of other persuasions, shall also thoroughly understand it. I have purposely not pushed the Bill because I was most anxious that every one should be thoroughly satisfied with it. Now, I think the time has come when I may proceed to a second and a final stage. My motion is seconded by Mr. Bell.

speechtext:
Before the business of the House is proceeded with, I may call to mind that some few days ago the bon. gentleman who leads the opposition asked the government to make some explanation as to the ministerial changes which have taken place recently. I thought at the time, if I may say so, that his request came a little too late for he had noticed the changes in his speech In the debate on the Address from the Throne, and he presented to the House his observations in regard to the matter, which on the whole were not at all unfavourable. But, if my bon. friend wants to have the subject re-opened, of course there can be no objection.
I have only to say, what is within tho knowledge of every one, that in the interval between last session and the opening of this session two vacancies occurred on the bench of the Supreme Court caused by the deaths of Mr. Justice King and Mr. Justice Gwynne. The government, in view of the situation, came to the conclusion that these vacancies on the bench would be worthily filled by Sir Louis Davies and the Hon. Mr. Mills. As to the qualifications of the Hon. Mr. Mills and of Sir Louis Davies it is needless to say anything in this House. They had both been for many years very valuable and trusted members of the House of Commons of Canada. Mr. Mills was one of the oldest of our parliamentarians ; he having sat continuously, with the exception of one session, either in one branch of the legislature or the other, since confederation. Of his legal abilities, and of his constitutional talent aud knowledge, we who are his old colleagues in this House have had many and many evidences.
Sir Louis Davies after having served an honourable career in liis own province came to this House for tlie first time in 1882, and be immediately took a leading and commanding position wbicb be retained to the end of his parliamentary career. Those who have been members of parliament and in public life for a great many years, know that tlie responsibilities which are involved in this country by the discharge of parliamentary duties are very exacting and very absorbing in their nature, and that they tend to produce a strain uftmi tlie system which it is hard to bear. There comes a craving at a certain period of life for rest -not absolute rest, at all events that comparative rest which is to be found in the performance of duties which are not so absorbing. Had it not been for this consideration, for my part I would have hesitated very much before thinking of offering these gentlemen a position on the bench, because I realize as parliament must realize also, how much the government and parliament loses by their absence. Nobody can realize how much I shall lose personally, having

had their valuable support since it was my privilege to become the leader of the Liberal party in Canada. However, these considerations were put aside and we thought we owed it to these veterans ill public life to call them to a sphere where their services would be of a different nature but still equally profitable to their country. But what parliament will lose the bench will gain. As to the fitness of these two gentlemen for the position to which they were called, I have not heard a word of dissent, nor do I believe that on this occasion there will be any objection raised. That they are eminently fitted for the positions they occupy was testified to, I am happy to say, by such a prominent member of the House as my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), and so far as Sir Louis Davies is concerned a tribute was paid to him by the hon. gentleman from Prince (Mr. Hackett) who has been a long life friend, although a political opponent of the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
The question then arose as to how the portfolios which' were vacated by the accession of these gentlemen to the Supreme Court bench were so well filled. Sir Louis Davies had been Minister of Marine and Fisheries from the formation of this government, and the administration came to the conclusion that we would recommend as a most fit and proper person to succeed him, the Hon. James Sutherland, member for North Oxford.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Hear, hear.

We believed that Mr. Sutherland was a most qualified person to discharge the duties appertaining to that important office. We knew Mr. Sutherland beforehand. He had been for two years a member of the administration without portfolio and during these two years the House has had on more than one occasion reason to appreciate his great administrative abilities, as the House had also occasion to appreciate for many years before the sterling qualities with which he is endowed.
Hear, hear.

This is the first time that the portfolio of Marine and Fisheries has been held by a gentleman who does not belong to the maritime provinces, but though the fishing industry in the maritime provinces is of very great importance, it must be remembered that there are other provinces in the Dominion which also have very great interests in that industry. The province of Ontario, if it is a second, is a good second to the maritime provinces in the extent of its fishing interests. Moreover, while -it is proper that the portfolio should be held by one who represents a province in which there is a valuable fishing industry, it is not to be disputed that it is fit and proper that in the representation in the
Cabinet all provinces should have a voice, and everybody will agree with me that the proportion as to the representation between one province and another province is not absolute, nor can there be a cast iron rule about it. Some elasticity must prevail according to time and circumstance, and I think that under the present circumstances the choice that we have made will not be criticized in any part of the Dominion.
With regard to the portfolio of Justice we came to the conclusion that nobody could fill it better than the hon. gentleman who for five years has been Solicitor General, and who has discharged the duties of that office not only with marked acceptance from both sides of the House, but with conspicuous ability.
Hear, hear.
We believe that although the portfolio of Justice has been held in the past by lawyers of very great eminence, the Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick will prove himself in every way their peer.
Hear, hear.

This left a vacancy in the office of the Solicitor General, and though the Solicitor General does not belong to the Cabinet, perhaps it may not be out of place that I should say that we thought of offering the position to a young gentleman from the province of Quebec, who has shown himself on every occasion that he addressed the House, to be a man of very great ability indeed. Mr. Carroll is Solicitor General.
Hear, hear.
It only remains for me to say that in view of the growing importance of the west, Senator Templeman has been appointed and sworn a member of the Cabinet without portfolio.
Hear, hear.

These are the changes that have taken place in the Cabinet, and such as they are we present them to the House with the full belief that they will command the support of our friends and challenge the criticism of our opponents.
It is perhaps better that a motion should be made. It is moved by Sir Wilfrid Laurier that the House do now adjourn.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask how the present government can reconcile these acts with the position of their colleague, the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock), in view of the fact that he placed on record a few years ago their opinion, that no member of this House should be appointed to a place of emolument under the Crown until at least two years after he had left the House.

That is something which is very easily explained. That is one of those falsehoods which have been started by some gentlemen on the other side, repeated by his neighbour, and then by him to his neighbour, and at last by everybody. The truth of the matter is simply this, that I think in 1894 or 1895, my hon. friend the present Postmaster General, who was then a private member of this House, introduced a Bill in the sense which has just been mentioned by my hon. friend from Grey. My hon. friend the Postmaster General thought, rightly or wrongly-for my part, I thought wrongly- that we should have that legislation on our statute-book. I never favoured it, nor do I know of a single member on this side of the House who expressed approval of it. My hon. friend the Postmaster General was in advance of the time. He received no support from the other side of the House. Hon. members opposite scouted his Bill, they would not vote for it, and it never came even to a second reading. It was read the first time, and never went beyond that, and the matter was absolutely for-

gotten until four or five years afterwards, wlien these lion, gentlemen sitting on the other side of the House thought fit to resurrect that old dead issue in the hope of making some political capital out of it. But I can say to my hon. friend that after all I am only flesh and blood, and I am satisfied to have the approval of the country for the changes we have made.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman if there is any truth in the rumour of the resignation of the hon. Postmaster General ?

I can assure my hon. friend that there is no truth in it.
Hon. DAVID TISDALE} (South Norfolk). Mr. Speaker, however the right hon. leader of the government may have answered the remark of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), I hope he does not deny that that position was a strongly advocated plank of the Liberal candidates throughout the province of Ontario. I really forget what happened to that Bill, but I know that a number of Liberals were in favour of it, and I know that throughout the province of Ontario, not only during the contest of 1891, but in 1887 and previously, one of the great subjects of complaint by Liberals was that the Conservative party were appointing members of parliament or men which had been members of parliament to offices of emolument. For my part, I am on record in ' Hansard ' in favour of doing so, because I am one of those who are willing to express their opinions, whatever they may be, upon all questions that come before this House. At the same time, it is perfectly proper-and that is one of the reasons why I rose at this time-to ask explanations from a party which in opposition advocated a measure on which a great principle was at stake, and in regard to which the electors of the country held very different and very strong opinions. It is very proper to recall to the recollection of hon. gentlemen a principle which they advocated when out of power, and which they abnegate when they are in power.
This is not a matter worthy of long discussion, but there is another subject on which I would ask leave to trouble the House in connection with these same appointments. Let me say that, so far as the two hon. gentlemen themselves are concerned, I have every confidence in their integrity and ability to fill the high positions to which they have been called. I think their appointments are excellent ones, but there is, in this respect, another high principle departed from entirely. In a session not long since, legislation was introduced to fix a limit of age, after which no one should be appointed. It was proposed to go even further and make this legislation retroactive. I opposed it because I considered that it would be a breach of faith on the 14
part of parliament to make ex post facto legislation with regard to gentlemen who had accepted positions under the law guaranteeing their retention of these positions during life. What more do we find ? We find the hon. the Minister of Justice declaring that he proposes to introduce this session a Bill fixing an age limit in the case of the county court judges of Ontario, and fixing a limit which would have prevented the making of one of the appointments lately made. I could not gather from the remarks of the hon. minister whether he proposed to make the Bill relating to the county court judges retroactive or not, and I wish to place myself on record as opposing any such proposition. Why should he deal with the county court judges of Ontario and not with the judges of other courts ? Why is Ontario specially singled out, whose county court judges are in every way capable ? And if you are going to apply any limit to the county court judges, you should make the same limit apply to the higher judges. Were you to apply to the Supreme Court the age limit, which it is proposed to apply to the county court judges, you would render the last gentleman appointed to the Supreme Court bench ineligible for the position.

My hon. friend was not in the House when I made a few remarks a day or two ago with reference to prospective legislation affecting county court judges, and I know him to be an extremely fair minded gentleman who would not willingly misrepresent any statement made in this House. My hon. friend must bear in mind that there never was any intention to introduce exceptional legislation with regard to Ontario. Any legislation that may be introduced with respect to the county court judges must be made applicable to all such judges throughout the Dominion. With respect to the other question, as to whether or not similar legislation might be made applicable to the High Court judges, I drew attention to the fact that the county court judges hold their office under an entirely different tenure, and while we have no right to interfere in any way with the High Court judges, we have special jurisdiction by statute with respect to county court judges. In any event there is no desire to interfere at all unnecessarily with any judges. On the contrary, my desire is to respect the bench in every particular, to hold absolutely sacred the position of judges. But at the same time, while I hold their position sacred, it must be borne in mind that the public have certain rights and that it is no advantage to the bench that men should occupy positions there for which they are admittedly not qualified. With respect to the age limit, it was intended to provide a limit which would vary from seventy to seventy-five years, coupled with a tenure of office of at least twenty-five years. And in



addition it was suggested that the change should be made optional, so far as the High Court judges are concerned, because we could not make it compulsory with them. With respect to county court judges, if a man has reached the advanced age of from seventy to seventy-five and has in addition been twenty-five years on the bench, to allow him to retire on full pay would not be a very great hardship.

subtopic: COMMISSIONS TO CANADIAN OFFICERS IN THE BRITISH ARMY.

speechtext:
Mr. HENRI BOURASSA (Labelle) (translation), moves for :
Copy of all papers and correspondence relating to the granting of commissions to Canadian officers in the British army.
Mr. Speaker, last year I moved a similar resolution to this one ; it was agreed to, on March 11th. On May 11th, I again moved for the production of those papers, and the government gave me the formal promise that they would be brought down as speedily as possible, but it was only on the day before prorogation that I got a certain number of the documents called for. I have now before me papers brought down last year; and they came partly from the Department of Militia, partly from Ri-deau Hall. In the file coming from Rideau Hall is to be found, a telegram dated March Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
31st 1900, from Mr. Chamberlain to His Excellency, in which reference is made'to two despatches sent by His Excellency to Mr. Chamberlain, the first one dated March 20th, the other dated March 30th. The latter is not to be found in the return. It seems but fair that, having the answer, we should also have the question which called for that reply.
In the other file, I find a despatch from Mr. Chamberlain to Lord Minto, dated April 9th, in reply to a despatch from His Excellency, of April 6th. Well, I should like to have the despatch of His Excellency to Mr. Chamberlain, which has given rise to the reply of the latter. On April 19th, Mr. Chamberlain wires again to Lord Minto, replying to a despatch of April 15th. Here again, we have the answer ; but the telegram which called for this reply we have not. Then comes another despatch dated April 27th, from Lord Roberts, the then Commander-in-chief of the troops in Africa, to His Excellency the Governor General, in reply to a despatch of April 17th from His Excellency to Lord Roberts. The latter despatch is not to be found in the return, Then we have a despatch from Mr. Chamberlain to Lord Minto, dated May 17th, in reply to a despatch from His Excellency, dated April 18th. That despatch of His Excellency is missing from the return. Then comes a despatch sent by Lord Minto to Mr. Chamberlain, on November 25th, 1900, which reads as follows :
It will be recollected that Her Majesty's government originally offered 30 commissions, and it was arranged that of these 24 should be allotted to Canadian troops serving in South Africa, the nominations to be forwarded to me by Lord Roberts, and submitted by me to the War Office, and the remaining six gentlemen of the Canadian Militia not serving in South Africa, recommendations to be forwarded by myself to the War Office.'
So, in this despatch, reference is made by His Excellency to arrangements entered into-between what parties ? I do not know. How those arrangements were made is another matter as to which we are left in the dark. Under these arrangements, the terms on whicli Canadian officers were offered commissions in the English army seem to have been altered.
If we are to be enlightened as to that matter, the whole correspondence must be brought down.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are met with a very important question here. Last session, I raised that question ; but as it was on the eve of prorogation day, and as from want of time, I could not use the phraseology required by parliamentary etiquette, I recollect, Mr. Speaker, that you called me to order ; but it is desirable that we should once for all come to an understanding on the point I am now referring to.
That His Excellency the Governor General does occupy a position in this country
421 FEBRUARY 26, 1902 422	
which is perfectly identical to the position occupied by the Sovereign in Great Britain or, by sovereigns in countries where a representative form of government like ours obtains, is a fact that no member in this House questions. But if we are to take any stock in what well recognized writers on parliamentary law state, the inference to be drawn is that the conduct of the Governor General was not always what it should have been, for one who really occupied the position of a constitutional sovereign. We have been told over and over again that the Governor General is the chief of the Canadian executive, the representative of the British Crown. In that capacity, of course, His Excellency plays in this country the part acted in Great Britain by the King. I do not wish to drag in the personality of His Excellency, which I am forbidden to do by rule 13 of this House, not to mention the rule imposed by good breeding in such matters, But I think, Sir, that if the constitutional rule laid down by Todd and several other authorities in parliamentary procedure holds good ; namely, that His Excellency is in this country both the chief of the executive and the representative of the British Secretary of State for the Colonies, there is, so to say, a dual personality in His Excellency. As chief of the Executive, he is, just like the chief of the Executive in England, liable to err. If the conduct of His Excellency is open to blame, that blame I have to cast upon the Governor General's advisers, namely, his responsible ministers. But when we come to deal with the representative of the Colonial Office, with the employee of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain, the Secretary of State for the Colonies, I think the representatives of the people of Canada have the right to criticise his course of action and to say whether the acts of the functionary of the British government, as well as the acts of the colonial secretaries, are deserving of blame or not. From that two-fold doctrine it follows that the Governor General is playing a very dangerous rdle when he seeks shelter under his prerogatives as the representative of the British Crown. So the Governor General could establish two classes of papers, in his files : he could give publicity to such documents as he might think fit to communicate to parliament, and in the same breath, assuming the rfiie of an employee of Downing Street, he could withhold other documents and say : ' For these papers I am not responsible to the people of Canada, as they refer to my secret relations with tfce Colonial Office.' Within the last two years this question has been threshed out in the Canadian press. On several occasions, if we are to believe press reports, differences of a rather serious nature have arisen between the Governor General and his ministers, either in connection with the sending of troops to South Africa, or as to the production of such 14J	papers as I have just referred to. Later on, last fall, similar controversies are said to have occurred upon the occasion of the distribution of medals and decorations bestowed by the Crown upon the Canadian subjects. The ministers are said to have claimed the right of advising His Majesty's representative as to the bestowal of such rewards. That such a doctrine is a sound one I firmly believe. We have been told that His Excellency, using a prerogative which the King himself does not dare arrogate to himself in his own kingdom, and relying upon his dual responsibility, did exercise the right of awarding decorations to whomsoever he pleased. In the matter of decorations, whether medals or titles or other knick-knacks of the same kind, I confess that I remain perfectly indifferent. But here, what is at stake is the production of papers which would materially help us to understand whether, in this matter of sending out troops to South Africa, and of enlisting volunteers, two years ago, and again last fall, the advisers of His Excellency did really take action with proper freedom ; whether His Excellency did consult them on all those points, or whether, His Excellency thought it expedient-always assuming that dual personality referred to above-to act now the role of a representative of the Crown, now the part of a representative of Downing Street ; seeking above all to safeguard the interests of the mother land and leaving it to his advisers to watch over the interests of the colony. Such is the question which now confronts us. And while I call for this return, I should like the right hon. the Prime Minister to throw some light on a point which affects very materially his constitutional position, as also the relations which should exist between the Governor General and his advisers, and the broader relations which should exist between Great Britain and her colonies. I often heard the right hon. Prime Minister claim as his leader-Sir Louis Hypolite Lafontaine, and I may say that whenever he referred in such eloquent terms to that political fathership, I cheered him to the echo. Now, Mr. Speaker, Lafontaine did not hesitate to provoke a ministerial crisis, even at the risk of bringing Canada to the verge of rebellion, and why, Sir ? It was in order to have it settled once for all, whether the people of Canada, like the English people, were free to manage their own affairs without any foreign power having the right of interfering with their domestic policy. The debate which culminated into the breach between Lord Metcalfe and Lafontaine grew out of a very trivial circumstance: namely, the appointment of a deputy-sheriff for the county of Carleton. But, to quote Lafoutaine's words, the question was as to whether the Governor was to be advised by his ministers or not ; the question was as to whether the people of Canada were free to

manage tlieir own affairs, reserving to tlie sovereign the allegiance which is the bounded duty of every portion of the British empire, without the Governor having the right to assume when it pleases him the functions of an agent of the Colonial Office and to exercise a dual personality.
I am led to think, Mr. Speaker, that the question was discussed by His Excellency and his advisers, from the fact that in the first despatch from Mr. Chamberlain to Lord Minto, dated March 20th, 1900, the following occurs :
' The Secretary of State far War offers four Royal Artillery eight infantry commissions to students Royal Military College, Kingston, recommended by Commandant as in every way suitable, ten Royal Artillery twenty infantry to gentlemen selected by your coming Imperial Officer Commanding local forces.'
So, as the House will see, Mr. Chamberlain pointed out that those commissions were to be given to gentlemen recommended by the commandant of the militia.
In another despatch sent by Mr. Chamberlain to Lord Minto, on the 9th of April, in reply to that despatch of the 6th April, which is missing from the return, I read what follows :
' Referring to your telegram of April 6th re the selection of candidates for commissions, the candidates should he recommended by you after consulting with /our Ministers and Imperial Officers.
" You should communicate to your Ministers suggestion contained in your confidential despatch of 24th ult. as to Board for wise selection of candidates, and list should be submitted to you through your Ministers with their recommendations. Responsibility for the final selection remaining with you."
,	(Signed) CHAMBERLAIN.
What happened between March 20th and April 9 ? Whether there was controversy between His Excellency and his constitutional advisers is more than I can say. But I incline to the belief that the matter was discussed between them, and that His Excellency then wrote to Mr. Chamberlain for his opinion, and that the Colonial Secretary thought it wiser to split the difference. The selection of the officers he left to the ministers, or rather, he advised the Governor General to Invite the opinion of his advisers on this point, adding that responsibility for the final selection remained with the Governor General. Neither can it be questioned, from the tone of the first despatch of Mr. Chamberlain, that His Excellency was free to take action after asking the sole advice of the officer commanding the Canadian militia.
A constitutional question is at stake here of the utmost Importance. To ascertain on what point the controversy then turned is the question. It is desirable that the issue should be clearly defined as between His Excellency and his advisers.
After a debate, the first and last landmarks of which we have, hut the Inter-

speechtext:
mediate stakes of which are missing, as showing the route travelled over, it stands to reason that there was a difference of opinion ; for, otherwise, how are we to account for what, apparently, has transpired ? What is the position which the government occupies towards the representative of Downing Street ? That Canada is a nation, enjoying the full privileges of self-government is a boast we are now familiar with. But the question which is now being raised is one that bears upon the relations existing between the irresponsible representative of the Crown and his constitutional advisers. The question which now confronts us is this : whenever there arises a question as to which the interests of the Canadian people and the interests of the English people clash, ought not the Governor General to refer the matter to the cabinet, which is the sole medium of communication between His Excellency and the will of the people, and should he not act upon the advice of his ministers ?
This doctrine Australia for one, upholds. What happened, last fall, in that colony ? Bills concerning immigration, trade and navigation were brought up and carried through parliament. The bill on immigration had been framed on the lines of the bill carried through the legislature of British Columbia in connection with Mongolian labour and immigration. Mr. Chamberlain wrote to Mr. Barton, the Prime Minister of Australia, asking him to commit himself to have this Act amended, so as not to create bad blood in Japan, a country with which Great Britain was seeking to make a treaty. In the same despatch, it was recommended that the Act respecting trade and navigation should be amended, so as not to interfere with the interests of the great British companies which were engaged in trade with Australia. Mr. Barton replied through the Governor General, Lord Hopetoun, simply promising that he would do his best to comply with the wishes expressed by Mr. Chamberlain. The Australian parliament was called together, and the first debate that was raised in the House at the beginning of the session, turned on the very question whether the Prime Minister had been warranted in writing to Mr. Chamberlain that he would endeavour to have the Act modified, which was mentioned in the despatch referred to, so as to make it tally with the interests of the mother country. The opposition leader, Mr. Reid, strongly criticised the government because the premier had assumed upon himself to send an answer to Mr. Ghamberlain's despatch before first ascertaining the views of parliament. From Mr. Reid's firm attitude, Mr. Barton was frightened into notifying Mr. Chamberlain that he could not comply with his wishes.
What happened in Canada ? Following in the footsteps of Australia, British Columbia had passed a bill regarding Mongolian la-

bour and immigration. Into tlie merits or demerits of that legislation I do not wish to go. Let it suffice to say that the provincial legislature, in passing that measure into law, acted within their constitutional jurisdiction. And this measure it was at the demand of Mr. Chamberlain that it was set aside by a Liberal government, a government the members of which formerly stood up here and championed provincial rights. The Dominion government did not hesitate to blot out from the statute-books of a province of Canada an Act passed by the legislature of that province, in the full exercise of their constitutional prerogatives.
On the floor of the Australian parliament, Mr. Reid has laid down this principle, that no prime minister of a British colony, enjoying free institutions, has the right to ' enter into relations with the Colonial Qffice and to communicate to the same his policy, whether actual or contemplated, before having first secured the assent of his parliament. To quote Mr. Reid's own words : ' The prime minister of Australia is responsible to the people and the parliament of Australia, but he is neither responsible to the Colonial Secretary nor to the British parliament.'
It was not my intention to have gone into the matter in all these details, nor to have spoken at such great length, but this I am bound to say, that after having been in waiting four mortal months for this correspondence, and after having received but a garbled correspondence, while, as I have pointed out, the Governor General's answers to despatches have been withheld, I think I am warranted in hoping that more light will be shed on the matter by the government bringing down the documents which have been withheld, so that our doubts may be cleared up as to the relations which ought to exist between the Governor General and his advisers.

For instance, let us suppose that one of these dispatches referred to the arbitration which was at that moment going on between Russia and Great Britain regarding certain seizures of our vessels which were made a few years ago by the Russian authorities. (Translation.) Before this motion carries, I wish to offer one or two remarks. Does the hon. member for

Labelle mean to stand up on the floor of this House as the champion of popular rights V Can he say with the French poet:
' Je suis venu trop tard dans un monde trop vieux.'
Or, again, has the hon. gentleman mastered the elementary principles of the British constitution ? Had he been conversant with the principles by which our parliament is guided, as well as all other parliaments in which a constitution obtains which is based on constitutional principles similar to ours, he could, to say the least, have dispensed with going at such great length into a review of an uncontested right, and one which no member of this House who is conversant with the principles of our constitution, would even dream of questioning. The hon. gentleman no doubt forgot in addressing the House that on both sides, and even among his friends and colleagues, are to be found, men who are acquainted with these principles as well as I am, and who, being his elders know better than he does what those principles mean. After all this is a motion to which, according to British parliamentary rules, no objection could be raised.
It refers to militia matters ; it refers to the commissions granted to Canadians in the British army. The hon. gentleman in dealing with this matter, indulged in much hair-splitting. To his mind, His Excellency the Governor General now represents the Crown, now represents something else. The Governor General represents the King, and, at the same time, he is the servant of the people of Canada. Then, the hon. gentleman, launched out, with great flourishes, into a recital of our long-continued struggles for the conquest of our rights. That the Governor General in Canada represents the Crown ; that he discharges a dual function, namely, as the representative of the Crown on the one hand, and as an official of the English government on the other hand, everybody here is aware. But no matter how you may look at the question, can there be any doubt, or has any one ever questioned our rights to control our own domestic affairs ?
A mere glance at the constitutional history of England is sufficient to satisfy us that there is no room for the least doubt in the matter. Only to such people as are not conversant with that history can it occur that we are without the right of self-government here. But, for our part, we know that history, and I would advise my young friend from Labelle to peruse the three volumes written by Mr. de Franqueville on the British constitution, and he will find there that we are enjoying the right of self-government. Does the hon. gentleman wish to pose in this House as the champion of our blood-bought liberties, within the last centuries ? This motion refers to military matters. Now, these matters come under the

direct control of the British parliament, and [DOT]the same applies here. This control was secured long ago, with the abolition of the ' Mutiny Act.' In the Middle Ages charters, it is expressly provided, that the people of England, through their parliament, shall have the control of all military matters. Under the ' Bill of Rights ' and the 1 Act of Settlement ' of 1701, ail military matters are placed under the control of parliament. This was a recognized right from the reign of William of Orange. For many years, the ' Mutiny Act ' had to be resorted to, in order to give a further sanction to the principle that parliament which appropriated the public moneys, also had the sole control of military matters. But the * Mutiny Act ' is a thing of the past. And the hon. gentleman laboured to no purpose, when reviewing the conduct of Governor Metcalfe and the history of those times.
Should any one dream of re-enacting now the ' Mutiny Act,' well might he compare with Rip Van Winkle who slept for twenty years, and never knew what had transpired within that lapse of time. A motion such as the one proposed by the hon. gentleman, would carry without any objection being raised to it, in the British House of Commons. In that House it would not even be debated, there being so many useful and practical questions which come up for discussion, and owing also to the fact that this right of control of parliament is so uncontested a right that nobody would ever dream of calling it in question.

speechtext:
That in the opinion of this House the [DOT] Table of Precedence for Canada,' as set forth in the Statutes of Canada and ' Canada Gazette,' should be amended either by omitting section 11, ' Archbishops and Bishops according to seniority,' or by giving a place in said section 11 ' to the clergymen of religious denominations other than those having '	" archbishops and bishops," the word ' seniority ' to be interpreted by ' territorial ' area, or in some other appropriate manner, and in other ways.
He said :	In making this motion I will
state briefly that in doing so I have no bias whatever. We find in the Dominion of Canada, where there is no union of church and state, that last autumn as well as on a former occasion of considerable political importance to this country, precedence was given to the members of certain churches over equally prominent, equally cultured, equally good and equally noble minded men of other churches in this country, although, as I say, there is no union of church and state here. I do not need to make any apology for introducing this question. The custom of recognizing the clergy in the table of precedence is undoubtedly a relic of old times, of former days, when there was a union between church and state. It is a relic which possibly does no harm and which, so far as Canada is concerned, may be allowed to continue, only I maintain that all the great denominations in this country should be equally recognized. It has been stated that my motion is not in the right form, that I should have moved that a humble petition be sent to His Majesty and to the Imperial Executive. I do not think that is the proper course at all in this connection. I have taken the course of presenting the facts to the House, of presenting my views to the House, of bringing the subject before the House, and if it meets with the approval of the House, as I am satisfied it will meet with the approval of this country, then it becomes the duty of the Prime Minister to lay the matter by petition before the Imperial authorities, asking them to make a change.
It has been stated that this is a personal matter with His Majesty the King. I need not tell an intelligent legislative body such as this that His Majesty the King has no personal authority in such matters whatever. A great many people are under the misapprehension that His Majesty, or His Excellency the Governor General, in his individual capacity, has certain prerogatives in certain circumstances. They have none. When the question of purchase of commissions in the British army was done away with, people were told that it was one of Her Majesty's own personal prerogatives that was exercised. But she exercised that prerogative with the advice of her responsible ministers. The Sovereign, or His Excellency the Governor General, have no prerogative other than as they are advised by the Prime Minister in Great Britain or in this country. The statement that the sovereign, being the sole fountain of honour, has absolute control of this matter is not borne out by either law or custom under the British or Canadian constitutions. These tables have been changed from time to time on petition, possibly not in this colony, although I believe that in this colony they have been changed. On representation from the people in the various colonies concerned they have been changed, and they may be changed, and should be changed again. I shall not discuss the question at any length further than to reiterate that if the government of this country sees fit they can petition the Imperial authorities to have the table of precedence changed in order to include the leading ministers of other churches, gentlemen equally prominent, equally cultured, equally noble, equally good. I make no reflection on those of any church that is now recognized. I say if the government make a proper request to the imperial authorities there is no doubt that the request will be acceded to. and we will find that the various non-prelatical churches will be recognized in the table of precedence along with those already recognized. I need not say that the table as at present constituted is offensive to many of the denominations that are recognized on account of their desire to see all parties recognized. It is offensive in the fact that it gives some churches prominence while it does not recognize others. I shall conclude the few remarks that I purpose making upon this question by reading one of many letters which I received from prominent clergymen and others throughout the country. I read this one because it is a copy of a letter which was forwarded to the Prime Minister some time ago by a very prominent ecclesiastic. It is as follows -
Montreal, October 28, 1901.
The Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, G.C.M.G., Premier of the Dominion of Canada,
Dear Sir,-In the matter of ecclesiastical precedence at state functions in Canada, permit tne to approach you in a spirit of candour without narrowness and with a desire to avoid religious agitation by public discussion. I wish to present this matter in the same broad minded spirit with which I have tried to consider any public question in which I have been interested. As a resident of this province where I have spent most

I cannot complain of the manner in which the question has been brought before the House by my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria). The question itself is not of very great importance, but unfortunately it is one of those questions which have created a good deal of friction at different times in the history of confederation. I must take issue at once with the statement made by my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes), that the government of Canada-whatever government may have been in power-is responsible for the present condition of things. As a matter of fact the authority which is responsible for the present table of precedence is not in Canadsf, but in England, and it is His Majesty the King. The Governor General is not a free agent in this matter, I may say. It is not permitted to him to follow his own inclinations as to what degree of honour he shall give to those whom he invites to his table, but he is instructed from England as to how he shall proceed in all state ceremonies, and as to how he shall seat those who are his guests. The present table of precedence is, I believe, as
old as confederation, although modified since in a very slight degree. Before confederation the instructions as to precedence went back as far as the union. For my part I am of opinion that the dissenting churches have good reason to feel aggrieved at the manner in which they have been treated in this respect, the feeling became more acute at the time of the visit of the Prince of Wales. I believe, however, that the churches are somewhat to blame if they find themselves placed in that position. For thirty years or more, the bishops and archbishops of the Episcopal churches-in this country the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of England-have alone been recognized in the table of precedence.
I would not offer my own interpretation of history in this matter, but if I have correctly interpreted history, my impression is that in former times the dissenting churches did not seek any such recognition as is now sought by the motion of the hon. gentleman. Whether they were right or wrong it matters not, because if at the present time the rfissenting churches wish to be recognized in this country they ought to be recognized. There can be no doubt as to that. I would point out that the difference in this respect between Canada and Great Britain is all to the advantage of Canada. In Great Britain the Church of England is alone recognized.
No.
I think so. Mr. HUGHES (Victoria). Roman Catholic bishops are also recognized.

If the Roman Catholic bishops are recognized in Great Britain, it is I think by tolerance and not by established rule. But whether or not the Roman Catholic Church is recognized there, I think I am safe in saying that the dissenting churches are not recognized in the table of precedence. There is a reason for that. In England they have a state church, and in Canada all churches are on a footing of equality. I have no hesitation at all in stating my convictions; convictions which are not mine alone, but which I share with, I am sure, every member of this House. I must say to the hon. gentleman that the task of framing a table of precedence which will give proper recognition to all churches is very difficult and is surrounded with serious intricacies. For instance, the question arises:	Which church
shall be given precedence over the other. The letter which was addressed to me some months ago by the Rev. Dr. Shaw, of Montreal, would indicate, if I understood aright the reverend gentleman, that precedence would be given to the Lutherans, because he said that if you look upon it from the point of view of antiquity, the Lutherans should come first. The Lutherans are a small body in Canada, and although I do

not know that the Rev. Dr. Shaw meant they should get precedence, at all events it was a suggestion which he submitted for our consideration. In the Roman Catholic Church and in the Church of England the dignitaries of these churches are permanent officials, but when you come to the Presbyterian Church, or the Methodist Church, or the Baptist Church, the difficulty is to recognize who are the proper dignitaries. Dignitaries in that sense they have none; they do not admit the term I believe, but they have certain officials. The Presbyterian Church has a moderator, which if he does not change annually at all events changes frequently. Who shall be placed on the table of precedence as representing the Presbyterian Church ? Should it be the moderator, whose tenure of office is comparatively brief. I understand that the Methodist body have certain functionaries who are also elected for a fixed term. As to the Baptists, I understand that their organization is absolutely democratic, that they recognize no such rule of precedence amongst themselves, and that thfly have no functionaries corresponding to those in the other churches. It would, therefore, be very difficult to place the representative of the Baptist Church upon the table of precedence.
I may say to my hon. friend that all these difficulties have been looked into by the government. At the time of the visit of the Prince of Wales we knew there were very serious complaints from some eminent divines of the disseneting churches in this and other cities. They complained very strongly that they had been ignored and had not been extended the courtesy which was extended to the dignitaries of the other churches. The government was not callous to such representations. A sub-committee of the council has been appointed to look into this matter and to prepare a report. It is now under investigation. I repeat to my hon. friend, that when we come to the point of framing a table of precedence such as we should have, the difficulty is almost insurmountable in finding a way to give precedence to those entitled to it. We are doing our best at the present time to overcome the difficulty. I would be very much obliged indeed if the mem* bers of this House would give us the benefit of their views as to what table of precedence we should recommend to His Majesty the King. At the present time we are very much in the dark, and we have not been able to arrive at a solution which we would like to recommend to the Imperial authorities. The matter shall not be forgotten by us. I hope, before this subject is dismissed, that members of the House, especially members who belong to the Dissenting churches will give us the benefit of their views on this subject so that we may be enabled to make representations to the proper authorities. I Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
agree with my hon. friend that the moment the parliament of Canada, represented by the government, makes proper representations to the Imperial authorities, these representations will be immediately acceded to.

If it be the case, as I understood the premier to say, that the Governor General received instructions as to precedence from the Imperial authorities, I have no doubt whatever that representation on the subject from any colonial authority would be received with attention, and that any wise suggestions coming from the Dominion of Canada or any other colony for overcoming the difficulty, would receive due weight. There is no doubt, from the information given us and from what we know, that this is a difficult question to settle and a delicate one to handle, especially in a country like ours, where many large dissenting denominations see other religious bodies given precedence over them. How would it do, in a democratic country like ours, to do away with all precedence in connection with these functions-to give no church any precedence over another, and thus do away with all ground for complaint ? That suggests itself to my mind as one way of overcoming the difficulty without doing injustice to anybody. The other suggestion made by the Rev. Mr. Shaw appears to have a good deal of merit in it, but there are objections to it which might be raised. I have no doubt that if it were known to the country that the government desired to consider this question, they would receive many suggestions from quarters from which they have not yet heard, and that after due consideration they would be able to evolve some scheme to meet the difficulty, which at present is a grievance, if not an offense, to some churches which are very numerous in certain sections of the country.

So far as I am concerned, I am rather democratic on this subject. In the first place, I wish to say, in reply to what the premier has said, that the office of moderator of the Presbyterian Church is continuous, just as the office of premier is, though the man who holds the office may change. For example, the man who is moderator this year may give place to another man next year, but the office is eternal, and Will be. For myself, if I had my own way, I would not have any precedence at all, either ecclesiastical or otherwise. There are of course certain persons, such as members of the government and members of parliament who represent the people, and if there is any distinction, and I do not ask for any, I can understand that it would only be right and just that places should be assigned to them, not as a matter of precedence, but simply to enable them to get their proper places. But in this democratic country I do not think we

want much of that kind of thing. I think : there are about thirty orders in the table of precedence. I have not looked over it lately, and do not intend to look at it again. An kon. MEMBER. Twenty-six.

Just imagine that in a democratic country-twenty-five personages or representatives of various communities who are ahead of you. I am not claiming the twenty-sixth place or the twenty-third, or any place; but 1 say it is absurd in a country like this. Personally I do not think the clergy need be recognized at all more than others. What I mean is this : X think they could be better employed in preparing men to be good citizens than in struggling for precedence over each other, and I think the democratic church to which I am attached is not making much of a cry about this matter. There is a way of settling the question which might not occur to the clergy, and that is the way they settled it in the British Columbia legislature the other day. But, seriously,
I think the churches should not say much on this subject. I can understand those who have dignitaries in their churches- Roman Catholics and Episcopalians-being interested in it; but if I might make a suggestion, I would say let the clergy imitate the men they represent, the humble fishermen of Galilee, and say : ' We are not after it at' all.' If they did that, they would show the greatest lesson of tolerance to the people of this country. My view is that we should become more democratic in this matter, and I would suggest to the premier that when the negotiations are on, he might strike off more than 334 per cent. If that is done, in a very few years we shall hear very little more about precedence in this country. If I remember rightly, Ur. Shaw proposes that precedence be given according to population. That is all nonsense. There are small bodies of people in this couutry who have shown themselves to be just as good citizens and as high in the scale as are the best. If you divide people in that way, you simply make precedence a question of majorities, and you shut out real merit and degrade the smaller denominations. Then, you would find this difficulty, that in one province precedence would be given to a man belonging to one denomination, and in another province to a man belonging to another. My suggestion to the premier is to recognize in this country very few of these positions at state functions. Let us all go to pay our respects, as we did when the Prince of Wales was here, feeling that character, and character alone, entitles a man to be there. Let us not be so anxious to set a man up in a high position just because he belongs to a particular church. These are my democratic views. Before I sit down, let me say, that I think this motion should not pass. It says : ' the word " seniority " to be interpreted by " territorial " area, or in some other appropriate
manner, and in other ways.' That would make it worse that it is at present.
Did I understand from the right lion. Prime Minister that the matter is now under the consideration of a sub-committee of the Privy Council ?
Yes.
Perhaps my hon. friend would let the motion stand for the present, having the right to renew it at a future time.
I have asked my hon. friend to withdraw his motion.

I wish only to remark that my hon. friend from Guysbor-ough, in claiming for the members of this House a more exalted position than they possess at present, hardly exhibits that humble spirit of the Galilee fishermen which he commends to the clergy.
I do not want a high position, but if I did, I think the twenty-fifth or twenty-sixth place for the leader of the opposition would not be according to his dignity.

I am not going to raise that question, although I suppose I should be very much obliged to my hon. friend for raising it for me. I can well understand the difficulties that present themselves to the Committee of the Privy Council in dealing with this matter; and when the Prime Minister tells us that the government are dealing with it, I think it would perhaps be inadvisable for us to pass any motion in the House with regard to it at the present time. As the right hon. gentleman tells us that his government are dealing with it, it would be better not to pass any motion now on the subject. After the government have dealt with it, this House can, by means of an address or motion, express its opinion on the conclusions arrived at.

In rising to withdraw this motion at the request of the Prime Minister, I may say that I am somewhat surprised that my hon. friend from Guysborougli (Mr. Fraser)-a gentleman learned in the law as well as in the academies-should seem unable to understand the English language. If he will read the last phrase attentively, he will find that it does not refer to ecclesiastical precedence, but to the very point which he himself has brought up, namely, to the place occupied by members of parliament in the general table of precedence. I trust therefore that my hon. friend will brush up his English grammer, and he will then probably revise his conclusions. Of course one can readily understand why the hon. gentleman should wish the table of precedence abolished, for if there were no such table there would * be no resisting his weight in the scramble i for a front place. The right hon. the First

Minister certainly misunderstood what I said if lie thought I said the Governor General had anything to do with establishing the table of precedence. That table, as are all the sources of honour, is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Sovereign himself, and I merely mentioned the Governor General, in order to meet the' argument advanced, that this is a matter entirely within his purview. He has nothing to do with any matter except as advised by the Prime Minister of this country. I understand that in the past a claim for jurisdiction in this matter has been made upon behalf of one of our Governor Generals, and I understand that within a very recent period, a Governor General claimed the right to appoint his aide de camp as a personal matter. This claim, however, was entirely unconstitutional, and in any case it has but a remote bearing on the subject before the House. I have no doubt that if the right hon. the Prime Minister will consult the parties interested, he will arrive at a solution of the difficulty and be able to establish a proper basis of precedence. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) that this whole table of precedence should be done away with. But I am satisfied that neither the Prime Minister nor the British government would request the Imperial authorities to withdraw precedence from those who now enjoy it. One of the Australia colonies once petitioned the British government to abolish the precedence given the clergy, and Her Majesty's government replied that such precedence could not be taken away from those who already held it. All the bishops then in existence should retain their precedence although it might not be continued to those subsequently appointed. Acting on the request of the First Minister and in view of the fact that this motion is receiving the consideration of a special committee of the Privy Council, I have much pleasure, with the permission of the House, in withdrawing it.
Motion withdrawn.
