LANCASTER (Lincoln) moved second reading of Bill (No. 3) to amend the Railway Act. He said : I may say at the outset that this is neither a new question in the country nor does my amendment seek to create an entirely new state of the law. The history of the legislation in regard to cattle guards and fences on highway crossings is shortly this. Until the year 1888 the liability to erect and maintain cattle-guards and fences at highway crossings rested on the railway companies absolutely. In that year the Railway Act was consolidated, and this matter was dealt with in the consolidation, and dealt with in such a way that the liability was not only made not absolute, but was disposed of in such a way as to leave practically no liability at all. The enacting portion of the section of the Railway Act which was in force until 1888 was ns follows :
The company shall erect and maintain cattle-guards at all highway crossings suitable and sufficient to prevent cattle and other animals from getting on the railway.
Those who consider the question at all will know that these words constituted an absolute liability. In the consolidation of the Railway Act in 1S88, this section was changed by adding the following subsection :
Until such fences and cattle-guards are duly made and completed, and if after they are so made and completed they are duly maintained, the company shall be liable for all damages done by its trains and engines to cattle, horses and other animals, not wrongfully on the railway, and having got there in consequence of the omission to make, complete and maintain such fences and cattle-guards as aforesaid.
As soon as that was passed our courts began to decide that no company was liable because of the qualified liability expressed in that section, because any cattle that were wrongfully on the railway would be cattle that had no right to be on the highway-in other words, what are known as animals running at large. In the year 1890 the subsection which I have just read was struck out, and the following subsection substituted :

If the company omits to erect and complete as aforesaid any fence or cattle-guard, or if, after it is completed, the company neglects to maintain the same as aforesaid, and if, in consequence of such omission or neglect, any animal gets upon the railway from in adjoining place where, under the circumstances, it might properly be, then the company shall be liable to the owner of every such animal for all damages in respect of it caused by any of the company's trains or engines; and no animal allowed by law to run at large shall be held to be improperly on a place adjoining the railway merely for the reason that the owner or occupant of such place has not permitted it to be there.
This provision has the same effect on the farmers or other inhabitants of the country as the amendment of 1888, and our courts have been obliged to decide that an animal is not in a place where it might properly be if it is running at large and therefore gets on the railway. It at once strikes anybody who gives any consideration to the matter that there is no need of a cattle-guard at all if the animal is not running at large, because if it is in the control of a human being it will not get on the railway, even if there is no cattle-guards there, unless there is contributory negligence on the part of the person in charge of the animal. The question is a very simple one. Why are cattle-guards required ? Not to prevent human beings from driving their cattle or allowing their cattle to get on to a line of railway, but to prevent cattle, which are not within immediate control, from doing so. No cattle-guards would be required were the animals always under control. Until 1888 the law stood as I am trying to make it now. Until 1888 railway companies were obliged to provide and maintain these cattle-guards, and it is only since all the larger railway companies secured their charters, under the law as it stood in 1888, and as I seek to make it now, that they got this amendment passed, first in 1888 and then in 1890, taking away the rights our people enjoyed when the railways were built. We often hear the plea put forth, especially by railway companies, that we must not do anything to interfere with vested rights. Well, Mr. Speaker, this happens to be a case in which the farmer clearly has been deprived of a vested right. The condition of affairs which existed, when our farmers were compelled, sometimes against their will, to give up portions of their land, to allow their farms to be cut up and dangerous conditions established, for the benefit of railway companies, has since been changed, and changed without their consent, and it is only right that this old condition of things should be restored. All the petitions that are flooding this House this session, although the session is still very young, show clearly that the farmers never gave their consent to this protection being taken away from them which existed in 1888. Innumerable petitions have been laid on the Table asking us to amend the

law and put it back where it was, as I am now seeking to do.
It is an essential principle of every law that it should be effective, that it should accomplish something which requires to be accomplished. Otherwise it is merely a travesty. I would like any hon. member to explain what common sense there is in an Act which provides that a railway company or anybody else must do a certain thing and then fails to provide a penalty for not doing it, except in the event of certain conditions which could not possibly apply.
The only reason that can be urged against the amendment I propose is that perhaps it is hard on the railway companies. I submit that there is nothing in that contention, but that I am simply putting things back as they were in 1888 when these railway companies constructed their lines.
Another argument used is that if this amendment were to pass, the farmers would allow their animals to run at large in order to get compensation, in case of accident, from the railway companies. But that is a very poor and a very unfounded opinion of the whole of our farming community. Our farmers do not want their animals to run at large, but in spite of every precaution they will sometimes get beyond control. A fence may be blown down by the wind or some stranger may leave a gate open or something else may be done, for which the farmer cannot be held responsible, and an animal get out on to the highway. On such a case it is only fair to oblige the railway companies to take the precautions against these cattle straying on to their lines, which they were obliged to do some twelve or thirteen years ago. Besides there is a section of the Railway Act which I am not touching, and which prevents a farmer recovering damages for the injury or destruction of any animal that occurs on the highway where it is crossed by a railway. If an animal is killed or injured at the point of intersection, its owner cannot recover any damages, and I submit that while we retain that section in our law, every farmer will be interested in seeing that his stock do not escape on to the highway, lest they might meet with an accident at these points of intersection.
The argument that to allow the owners of cattle to recover damages from the railway companies will be an inducement to our farmers to let their stock run loose, answers itself. If you pass the Bill which I now urge upon you, you prevent animals from meeting the train except at the point of intersection of the railway and the highway. For, the effect would be to make it necessary for the railway company to make proper cattle-guards. It may be said this is enacted in the present law. But there is no use in enacting that the railway shall do a given thing, if you do not punish them for not doing it. The only way to compel them to put cattle-guards at the highway 15*
crossing is to hold them liable in thewcase of injury to cattle that had strayed upon their track from the highway, no matter how they got across the cattle-guard. If this Act is passed and railways provide guards which the cattle cannot cross from the highway, the only place at which an animal could be upon the track would be at the point of intersection of the track with the highway. If you give effect to the argument of the railways that under such a law as I propose farmers may grow careless and allow their animals to run on a highway, thus causing the risk of the trains being thrown off the track, you must also allow for the fact that under this Bill, the only point at which a train would meet an animal would be at the point of intersection. On the contrary, as things are at present, the train is liable to meet that animal at any point of the road from terminus to terminus. Thus, the very argumeut advanced in behalf of the railways, if it be advanced in this House answers itself, and the fact is emphasized that the railways would be protected by this amendment in the very way they want to be protected. Now, the law of this country on this subject is very different from that of any other country where the circumstances are at all similar. All the states of the Union, so far as I have been able to ascertain-and I have learned about a majority of them-have laws, which, though worded more or less differently are, in effect, the same as our law was before 188S, and as I am now seeking to make it. Obviously, the reason is just what I have already said, that, if you do not make the liability absolute you cannot expect that cattle-guards will be provided that will afford proper protection. Now, to state a case-innumerable cases have occurred-let us suppose that an animal goes away without the consent of the owner and gets upon the highway. The law being what it is, we might assume that the railway company has not provided proper cattle-guards. Railway companies do not do anything they are not obliged to do unless there is some clear advantage to be gained, and I think it would be fair to assume that proper cattle-guards have not been made. But let us suppose that there are effective cattle-guards. The animal goes upon the highway until it reaches the railway. But, the cattle-guards being there, it will be discouraged from seeking to move along the track. It is in danger while it is at the point of intersection, but it is encouraged to continue on the highway Where there is no danger. That is the only risk the owner of the animal ought to run. Of course, under municipal law, the owner is liable to have the animal impounded, and all the steps taken that are necessary for the protection of the inhabitants of the locality. But, so far as the railway is concerned, I submit that the only risk that the owner ought to

run is, if tlie animal though encouraged to remain on the highway is injured while it is on the track. But if the proper cattle-guards are not provided, the animal is induced to turn upon the track, which, to the animal does not appear more dangerous than the highway. The owner ought not to he called upon to bear that risk. Therefore, I submit, that the Bill which X have proposed is one which ought to meet with the approval of the House. Now, it has been said in the country, during the discussion of this subject within the last year, that such a law as I propose might have the effect of reducing the rate of speed of trains, that, with cattle-guards constructed at the intersection of every highway the speed of trains could not be maintained. In the first place, I do not think that the fact that a train may be prevented from travelling as fast as it did five or six years ago ought, of itself, to be a reason why an injustice should be done to the inhabitants of the country who are obliged, in carrying on their affairs, to keep animals that may go upon the railway tracks if there are no cattle-guards. But, in the second place, from inquiries I have made, I find that this is after all, merely a question of expense. I understand that a cattle-guard can be made that will prevent cattle straying upon the railway and still will not interfere with the solidity of the track, if there is a little masonry about it. We know that the railways have to use a good deal of masonry in their works all over their lines, for culverts, bridges, and so on. If it be true that the railway must run its trains a little slower, or else put a little more expense in the construction of cattle-guards, I submit that that ought not to be regarded as an effective objection to the amendment I propose. The railways ought to bear that additional expense in order that the people of the country may be properly protected. I do not wish to trouble the House at greater length or to repeat in other forms -what I have, already said. I understand that several other gentlemen wish to speak on the Bill. But, in closing, I submit that in the true interests of the country this amendment ought to pass, and these provisions be restored to the place in the statute law which they had in 1888, in order that the people may have the protection which I have endeavoured in my humble way to explain, and to which they are entitled.

speakeroldname: Mr. PHILIPPE DEMERS (St. John and' Iberville).
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, let me congratulate the hon. member (Mr. Lancaster), who has just spoken, upon his initiative and perseverance. Although last year, the efforts of the hon. member were not rewarded with success, still this year, again, he comes forward with the same Bill. But happily for him, this question comes up before the House instead of before the Mr. LANCASTER.
Railway Committee. Owing to the several petitions that have been presented in support of the contemplated legislation, it will be no hard task for the House to take a decision. As remarked by the hon. gentleman, it is not the intention to impose new obligations upon railway companies, but merely to come back to the state of things that existed up to the year 1888, and was amended by the statute of 1890. The change brought about by the amendment of 1S90 was quite radical ; for, up to that date, railway companies were held responsible by the courts, whenever cattle wandered and loitered on the highway, near the railway tracks, which were not then provided with cattle-guards. After that amendment had been passed, legislation changed very rapidly, in the several provinces of the Dominion ; but in the province of Quebec, notwithstanding this amendment of 1890, the Court of Appeal decided that railway companies were responsible for all damages to cattle wandering upon the railway tracks, through neglect of providing proper cattle guards. Later on though, in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company vs. Cross, the Court of Appeal adopted the jurisprudence of the other provinces, so that at this moment, railway companies are perfectly free not to comply with the laws of the land. They are incurring no risks ; for, when, I ask, are those companies to be held responsible to the public, if not in cases where, through their neglect of providing proper cattle-guards, cattle will wander on the railway tracks, causing thereby damages ? It is the only case which might occur, and railway companies are not responsible.
So, that since 1890, we have a law on the matter, which serves no useful purpose. There is no question of saddling railway companies with new obligations, but merely of giving a fresh sanction to the law already existing. I do not believe that railway companies would suffer from this Bill.
In the constituency which I represent here, several farmers have suffered from accidents to their cattle, which were due to the absence of cattle-guards. When appealed to, the railway companies have haughtily declined remedying grievances. They would simply laugh at the petitions sent by several municipal councils, requesting them to erect cattle-guards.
Accidents will occur, so long as we shall not have placed a sanction upon the obligation which has always existed for railway companies to maintain cattle-guards at railway crossings. The House, I hope, will adopt the legislation proposed by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), and will thus give sanction to a law meant to protect the interests of farmers, which would be greatly imperilled were we to reject the Bill now before us.

The Bill introduced by my hon. friend is a very important one, and interests a large section of the people of this country. At the same time we know from experience that the question is a complicated one, and requires a good deal of consideration before we venture on an amendment. I do not see any objection to allowing the second reading of this Bill and referring it to the committee, so that it may be carefully considered, and that we may hear the parties interested. You will admit, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure the House will agree with me, that one is scarcely able to form an opinion with regard to the different points involved in this matter from the speeches that are made on the floor of the House; one is much better able to form such an opinion when he hears the matter discussed before a committee, and has an opportunity of asking questions and getting information with regard to the various points that have been, I admit, very ably dealt with by the hon. gentleman who has spoken on the Bill to-day. So far as I am personally concerned I will agree to the second reading of the Bill, with the understanding that it be referred to the Railway Committee for consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: While the usual custom has been to refer railway and telegraph Bills to the Railway Committee, and no doubt the minister who has made that proposal is in harmony with that custom, still I do not see any strong grounds for referring this Bill to the Railway Committee. It is an ordinary public Bill, and as ordinary public Bills, after their second reading, are usually dealt with in this House by being referred to the Committee of the Whole House, and as this is only a commonplace Bill of one clause, therefore I think the best place to consider it is in Committee of this Whole House. There is one reason why 1 would object to refer it to the Railway Committee, and that is the history of what has taken place in that Railway Committee. I do not desire to reflect in any way on that committee, yet I cannot Tefrain from thinking over a large number of important Bills that go to that Railway Committee and are killed there, and never find their way back to this House, Bills that are usually in the public interest. It seems to be the graveyard of very many important Bills that are in the interest of the public.

Will my hon. friend allow me ? I think perhaps there is a good deal in the statement that many Bills are killed in the Railway Committee, but I do not think there are nearly so many as are killed in this House when they are considered in Committee of the Whole. I know that many amendments of great importance have been carried through the House after
having been reported by the committee, but in my experience of twenty-two years in parliament I cannot remember any Bill having been introduced by a private member and become law without having been considered by a committee of the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am speaking with reference to ordinary Bills.
I am speaking of public Bills.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Bills promoted by private corporations come back from the committee all right, but public Bills relating to the rights of individuals as against railways
Public Bills I mean.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
My experience has been that these Bills sent to the committee rarely if ever come back to this House reported from that committee. Therefore, I am opposed to the reference on that ground. Under the old law people knew what their rights were in the event of any accident occurring through defective cattle-guards, but under new law those rights were taken away. The history of railways in this country has been a constant infringement upon those rights. But as soon as the law was amended, new conditions were introduced, and now it is something that every person is not conversant with. If there were a great deal of intricate legislation about this Bill that it requires an expert to understand, there might be a strong reason for sending it to the Railway Committee. But I do not think there is any good reason for sending this Bill to the Railway Committee.
Now arguments have been suggested and facts presented to show that one reason why this amendment to the law was made was because the old cattle-guards were dangerous. AYhen this Bill was being considered I asked the question :	Will the hon. member who holds that contention give us any data of the number of accidents which have taken place on account of these excavations for cattle-guards, and no cases were given, and I believe it was never attempted to prove to the House or to the committee that any considerable number of accidents occurred on account of these excavations for the old kind of cattle-guards. Therefore, if that be so, and I believe it is, I do not think the argument should hold good or be of any value. It is a fact that every farmer in the country knows, that where there is a railway crossing his farm the cattle-guard is of no value whatever as regards keeping cattle off the railway track. They will walk over it winter or summer as unconcernedly as if there was no cattle-guard there at all. They are only pieces of bent iron put so closely together that cattle can walk over them almost as on a floor. Well, the railway companies do not care, because there is a law which prevents cattle run-

ning at large within half a mile of a railway, and if the farmer suffers loss from his cattle running on the public highways within half a mile, he is liable to be prosecuted by law for allowing them to do so. If his cattle get off on the railway and are killed, he has no redress whatever, and has to sustain all the loss. I do not think it was ever intended that should be so, and in my judgment it is very unfair. There was very little discussion when this amendment was made to the law.
Does this propose to remedy that defect, so that when cattle on a railway crossing are killed the owner shall have indemnity ?	.
I do not know what the hon. gentleman means by a railway crossing.
Where the highway crosses a railway.

No, not at all, it is not intended that this is of any value to the farmer as enabling him to get compensation for cattle killed on the highway, that is his own lookout; but it is when cattle-guards are so defective as to allow cattle to travel over them and get on the railway ground or tracks. That is all the Bill is intended to do, that is what the old law did do, and that is what the farmers are deprived of to-day.- When their cattle travel as they do right over the cattle-guards on to the railway grounds and are killed, they have no redress whatever, and have to sustain the entire loss. I was going on to say that when this law was amended there was very little discussion on it. In fact it was explained by an expert railway lawyer, I think very adroitly, and information was kept in the dark which, if that committee had possessed, they never would have allowed that amendment to pass. But they did not see the aim of it, and they innocently allowed the amendment to pass, believing that it was for some good purpose. But when they found out afterwards that the cattle-guards were of no value in keeping the cattle off the track, and that when the cattle went over these guards and got killed the owner had no redress, and when a case came to be decided in the courts, then they saw where the law was defective and very naturally a clamour arose for an amendment. Once or twice before an amendment was introduced to put the law back to where it was before, but through adverse influences the Bill did not become law, it was killed. It was sent first to the Railway Committee and then to a sub-committee of the Railway Committee, and through some accident or otherwise-I do not know what it was-it was killed. I, as one member of that sub-committee, know that a notice of the meeting of that sub-committee did not reach me until after the sub-committee had considered Mr. SPROULE.
the Bill and reported it back to the main committee, reporting against the Bill. But whether that was the result of accident or design I am not prepared to say. At any rate, the Bill did not come back to the Railway Committee as having received its support, and consequently it was lost.
Now, we want to discuss it in this House for two reasons. The first reason is to let the country know what the representatives of the people are doing or what they are disposed to do to protect the innocent farmer whose property was expropriated from him in the first instance in addition to which the dangers were increased on his own property by virtue of the operations of the railway corporations, although they placed these cattle-guards on their line. If it were publicly known throughout the country that the representatives of the people are opposed to this, I think they would be reminded of it when they went back for re-election. Therefore, we want to discuss the measure as generally as possible. We want to ascertain the sentiment of the House on the question so as to see whether hon. gentlemen think that they are in duty bound to do what is right towards the farmers of the country, or whether they consider it to be their duty to look after the interests of the railway corporations.
Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule), be good enough to explain the difference between the law as it now stands in relation to the farmer and the Bill as proposed ?

Under the old law, if the railway company did not keep up an efficient railway guard, sufficient to keep cattle from getting on the track, and cattle went on the track and were killed, the railway company were liable for damages. To-day, all they are obliged to do is to keep up cattle-guards, not necessarily efficient ones, not ones to prevent cattle from getting on the track, and if a farmer allows his cattle to run and they get on the track and are killed he has no redress because the railway company have maintained the cattle-guard, whether an efficient one or not. Under the proposed amendment to the law if the railway company maintain an inefficient guard they are not liable for damages and the farmer has to suffer. Under the old law if the cattle-guard was not an efficient one the railway company were liable. We desire to discuss this question as generally as possible and if there are any reasonable objections against the Bill we wish to know them so as we may consider them. As the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) said, the farmer had the first rights in the country, his property was expropriated from him against his will, and if you expropriate property, as a principle, it is held that you must give compensation. Although you have given moderately fair compensation for the property, there are other rights which

the farmer should enjoy. A corporation to which the country has given the right t:o invade the right of domain of the private individual should not be allowed to bring about other conditions which make it more onerous for the farmer to carry on his daily work, more expensive, or more dangerous or more likely to incur loss to him. Now, if a railway corporation expropriate property they should not be allowed to run their railway over a farm and allow it to remain in such a way that the farmer's stock can at any time get on the track and be destroyed and he have no redress from the railway company. Unless they take every reasonable precaution to prevent the destruction of stock as a result of getting on the track, a railway company ought to be held responsible for the damage and be obliged to pay it. Therefore, this Bill, in my judgment, ought to become law, and I am most strongly opposed to sending it to the Railway Committee. I want to say one word in regard to another amendment made to the law a few years ago. That was an amendment which made the farmer liable if he allowed his cattle to run at large on the highway within half a mile of a railway. I always thought that a very unfair provision of the law and a very unreasonable one, and I hold that opinion still. In many parts of the country the farmers find their very best grazing ground on the highway.
A farmer should not be deprived of the advantage of grazing his cattle on the highway, where there is better pasture perhaps than in his own fields. In Vermont he has the right to the use of the highway to the centre of the highway. Our law is somewhat different here, but still, by common consent, farmers have been allowed to take advantage of the highways and to graze their cattle on them, but, if a farmer allows his cattle to graze on the highway within half a mile of a railway he is liable to have them impounded and to be mulcted in damages. I think this wrong and I hold that such a law should be amended.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. T. THOMPSON (Haldimand and Monck).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understood the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) to say that he would move that this Bill be referred to the Railway Committee of this Chamber, and when he does so I propose to support that motion. I feel it due to myself to give the House my reason for so-doing. I represent an almost purely agricultural riding, and there I practice my profession of the law, so that I think I am in some position to take an intelligent interest in the discussion now before the House. I wish to say that I have come to the conclusion that the farmers have in this matter a most substantial grievance and I believe that I voice the opinion of the majority of the members of this House when I say that before this session is over a substantial remedy they must have for that substantial grievance. Now, the point between the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) and the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Sutherland) is as to where this matter shall be fought out. It would seem to me undoubtedly a better course to fight it out in the Railway Committee than to deal with it here. Now, Sir, my reason for saying that will be apparent to almost every hon. member of this House even before I state it. Our chief functions are undoubtedly legislative, but in order to enact good laws there should be thorough previous investigation, and we have in the committee a chance of examining witnesses, of hearing experts on both sides and of gaining the best information possible. It is for this reason that I would like to see the matter investigated in the Railway Committee. As I have said before I am heartily in sympathy with the farmers in this matter and should it go to tlie committee I shall use every endeavour in my power to see that this Bill does not have one more tombstone put up to it in that committee, which has been called the graveyard. It seems to me that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has, to use a common phrase, been playing somewhat to the gallery in this matter. He has talked so much about wanting to go on record on the floor of this House. The insinuation is patent that we want to sneak off to a committee where there is no ' Hansard ' reporter in order that we may do there what we would be ashamed to do on the floor of this House.
I resent any such insinuation as that. I believe that the average member of this House is an intelligent man and that he is equally willing to do his duty in the committee or in the House. The hon. gentleman said that we must discuss the Bill here so that we might put ourselves on record. We have to discuss it here when it is reported from the Railway Committee, so that it seems to me that we can put ourselves on record by referring the Bill just as well as we can now by discussing it.
It may never be reported from the Railway Committee. That is the trouble.

The chances are this year that when this matter goes to the committee, owing to the sentiment in regard to it in the House, it will come back and we will have an opportunity of going on record. I know very well that ' trimmer ' is a name that no man would like to have forced upon him, but in my honest opinion compromise is in many cases honourable, and in the best interests of this country. We have not only the farmers to consider but also the travelling public, and let me say to my hon. friend from East Grey that the farmers form a very large per cent of the travelling public. Let us go to the committee and find out what is best to be

done and then as honourable men do It. In conclusion may I be allowed to quote a very apt French proverb : ' 11 faut mettre d'e l'eau dans son vin.'

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I think the amendment moved by the hon. member is in several respects, similar to the Railway Act in force in the province of Quebec. Should there be any amendments required, then I think it would be better to refer the Bill to the Railway Committee, for further consideration.
There are three parties interested in the subject matter of this Bill. One is the farmer, another the railway company, and the third is the travelling public.
What about the cow ?
Hear, hear.

We will leave the cow with the hon. member. As between the farmer and the railway company my sympathy is entirely with the farmer, but we have to consider the interests of the travelling public as well as the interests of the other parties, and we should be very careful before we make any changes in the provisions of the law as it exists to-day. There is a mistaken idea in the minds of many hon. gentlemen here with regard to this law. I think it can be demonstrated beyond peradventure that the law as it exists to-day is really the ^*at ll;ls been in force in Canada since 1857. It is all very well to work up our sympathies in favour of the farmer-and of the cow as one hon. gentleman suggests- and I dare say that some hon. gentlemen Jnaj sympathize with the railway company but we cannot shut our eyes to the fact that the welfare of the travelling public should have our sympathy also. The object of the present law has been-and it has been so declared by the decisions of our courts- to impose a mutual burden upon the railways and upon the farmers whose cattle must be kept off the track in order that no danger may arise to the passengers and ern-ployees on railway trains. That is the object ot the law, and that principle we must keep m view when we' are discussing this question. It is in my opinion a question which ought to go before the Railway Committee, and there be thoroughly discussed. The provisions of this Bill with regard to cattle-guards is one of very great importance. lo-day, upon the continent of America, there are not two railways which are using the same kind of cattle-guard ; in fact upon different divisions of the same railway ln 9anS,da, different kinds of guards are used. The old pit-guard has been put aside and every imaginable device has been tried by the different railways in order to protect their line. It is as much in the interest of the railway company as it is in the interest

of the general public that the very best and most effective kind of cattle-guard should be adopted. It does seem to me that it would be highly proper that a commission should be appointed for the purpose of inquiring into and deciding upon what is the most effective cattle-guard, and having decided authoritatively on that, we should put the law in force and see that it is used on every railway. If that were done good would be accomplished, but I doubt if any good can be achieved by our saying that an effective cattle-guard should be used, in view of the fact that different kinds of guards, all supposed to be effective, are being used now throughout the Dominion. Some of these guards which are the most effectual for the purpose of keeping cattle off the railway are the guards which are most complained of by the farmers because they are liable to injure the cattle. I therefore think that it is most desirable that this whole question should be discussed before the Railway Committee, notwithstanding the remarks made against that body by the hon. gentleman for Grey (Mr. Sproule). If some valuable recommendation could be made to this House, I believe the government would be only too glad to adopt the suggestion and to take such steps as will enable them to decide which is the best kind of cattle-guard that should be used throughout Canada.

There is another very important interest that has not been referred to in this case. We have heard of the interests of the lawyers, the farmers, the general public, the railway companies and the cattle, but nobody seems to have thought of mentioning the necessity for protecting the lives of the men engaged in operating the trains. I have been at the burial of too many of the engineers and firemen and brakesmen of the town in which I live, to let a Bill of this kind pass without seeing that the interests of thiS body are properly safeguarded. I have as much sympathy with the farmer as any man in this House, but I could give you instance after instance where train hands were killed on account of some careless people allowing their cattle to roam on the track at night.
Not farmers.

You rarely find a farmer's cow running at large. It is usually the cow of some poor loafer around the village which is let loose to get some pasture at night, and the next thing you know is that the fireman and the engineer are piled up in the debris and hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of property destroyed. I am anxious that every railway company should be compelled to maintain the very best kind of cattle-guard, but I believe also that there should be safeguards provided for the men who are obliged to travel on the railways, and who are at the

mercy of some careless fellow who turns his cow loose at night.

In the interest of the farmer, in the interest of the travelling public and in the interest of all concerned, I believe that the pit-guard is the only proper guard to use. I believe that the pit-guard would be entirely used by the railway companies but for the expense that it entails upon them. It is certainly the safest guard for a train to pass over if it is properly built, and it is certainly the best guard for keeping cattle and other stock off the track. I also believe that the floor of this House is the proper place to argue this Bill out.

I have had the honour to receive a petition from my riding praying that some legislation be passed by this House in reference to this question. We have three railways in the riding of Addington, and there is a universal demand in the district for improvement in the railway culverts. If it be in the interest of railways to make better guards I would like to know why the railway companies have not done so. In the district which I represent a great many cattle have been killed on the railways, and the farmers have had no redress. I will give you an instance. A drover was taking cattle to the railway station to be shipped, and in spite of his efforts the cattle got on the track because the cattle-guard was not sufficient to keep them back. A train came along and killed half of the cattle, but the poor man had no recourse in law against the company, because the law said that the cattle-guard was a safe one. It is neither just nor right to allow the railway companies to build such cattle-guards which are not safe for the farmers, and not safe for the people using the highway or travelling on the railroad.
I was on a train myself one day when cattle got on the track and nearly the whole train was ditched, but fortunately no one was killed. I would point out to the House that what is protection for the travelling public is protection for the railway companies and also for the farmers. The sooner we pass a law here forcing the railways to build proper cattle guards, the better satisfied will be the people of the country. Canada has helped railroads enough to ask them to make this small return towards the protection of our people, and I trust that a measure calculated to safeguard the rights of the public in this regard will soon become law.

I do not propose to discuss the principle of this Bill, but I wish to correct some statements which have been made in this House with reference to the Railway Committee. Some hon. gentlemen made remarks in reference to the Railway Committee which were both uncalled for and unjustified. I can remember all the changes in the Rail-1
way Act since it was consolidated in 1888. I remember that in 1888 when the Hon. Mr. Pope was Minister of Railways, some two or three weeks were given to a careful consideration of the Act in the Railway Committee, and afterwards a very thorough discussion on the Bill took place in this House. After that the only important railway Bills which I remember were the one introduced by the hon. member for Lincoln, and a drainage measure which indirectly affected the railways. With these two exceptions all the Bills relating to railways went to the Railway Committee and were considered by that committee. I wish to make this correction, because when an hon. gentleman assumes the responsibility of reflecting upon the Railway Committee, he should inform himself of the true action of that committee. This matter is one of importance to the farmers, and I also represent an agricultural constituency, and it is not fair to the other members of the Railway Committee that the hon. gentleman should speak of it as a dangerous place to which to send any important Bill. I say that the Railway Committee, irrespective of which party is in power, is a most competent, faithful, honest and wise tribunal. I have been a member of that committee for fifteen years. I have taken a great deal of pride in it, and I am glad to say that I know of no tribunal in the world which I would rather trust than that committee. It is not pleasant for me to have to say some of these things, but I do not propose to allow these reflections on the Railway Committee to go on the journals of this House without making my protest against them. I want to congratulate the acting Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) on having to-day pursued the policy which has always been pursued by the most illustrious leaders on both sides of the House. I want to congratulate him, because since his party has been in power, I have sometimes had to find fault with the minister. I have always contended that so long as we have a Railway Act, the responsible minister should always take charge of such matters and see that fair play is given to all parties; and the acting Minister of Railways to-day, in my opinion took the proper course, and ought to be supported in it. With regard to the grievance which has been mentioned, there is certainly a strong desire to agree upon some methods for meeting a very complicated case, where important and conflicting interests are concerned; and I am satisfied that it is desired on both sides of the House to deal with the matter in all seriousness. I do not approve of sending a Bill of this kind to a sub-committee. I opposed doing so last year although I sat on the special committee. I think we should send it to a committee that will give the time and patience necessary to understand the case, and then the House will accept its decision.

I would like to ask the hon. member what became of the Bills for the protection of railway employees that went to that committee and never came back, the Bill respecting ditches and water courses, which also went there and never came back, and the cattle-guard Bill ?

The Bill relating to railway employees is not of the same character as this, though not less important, and I have no doubt it received due consideration. I understand that the matter it dealt with was adjusted by some arrangement brought about by the government between the railway employees and the companies.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the very discussion which has taken place, and which is only in its incipient stages, shows the wisdom of referring this Bill to the Railway Committee. There is apparently as much diversity of opinion on this question as there is on the question of prohibition. The Bill is important, affecting as it does several interests. There is a strong grievance on the side of the farmers, and there may be questions of rights on the side of the railways and the public. In legislation of this kind it has always seemed to me that the wise course to pursue is to refer it to the committee which is supposed to deal with such matters. Therefore, I think this Bill should go before the Railway Committee. While I agree with some of its provisions, there is something to be said on both sides, and it should be threshed out there.

A Bill similar to the one now before the House was introduced by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) last session, and was sent to the Railway Committee. The Railway Committee referred it to a subcommittee, aud, if I remember rightly, the hon. member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) was on that committee, but did not put in an appearance, or if he did he voted against the Bill.
I was at every meeting of that committee.

Well, that sub-committee took no action in the matter, and the present Bill may be treated in the same way. This is a very important question. The farmers have rights, and we are bound to make the railways and all other classes respect those rights, and I think it is time that this very important question was decided upon. This House has been flooded with resolutions asking it to take action, and if you were to have all the committees you please, you would not be any better informed on the question than you are to-day. Every man in this House knows all* about a cattle-guard. I Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
do not think any more light can be thrown upon the question than we all have this evening; and, I for one, think the question should be brought before this House here and now.

I rise to say, in the first place, that I am opposed to the suggestion that this measure should be referred to any committee other than the Committee of the Whole House, the representatives of the people. I do not think we can get any better light upon it than can be shed by the experience and knowledge of the various members of this House. It is not a new question, nor is the amendment a new one. It was brought to the attention of the House last session, and I think I am right in assuming that every hou. member of this House has given it careful attention in the meantime. Now, I hardly anticipated that I should find the hon. member from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) and the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) together on any question. I regret that the hon. member for Victoria is not in the good company we usually find him. The argument of these two hon. gentlemen is the same :	The object of the law is the
safety of the public and the safety of the railway employees. Why, Mr. Speaker, these hon. gentlemen cannot have been giving careful consideration to the amendment which has been proposed or the speeches which have been made this afternoon, or else they would know that it is for the greater safety of railway employees and the greater safety of the public as well as the protection of the farmer that the amendment of the hon. member for Lincoln is introduced.
The Bill does not propose to deal with the danger of a collision at the intersection of a highway and a railway, but we have the additional danger that along every mile of a railway, where proper cattle-guards do not exist, there is the probability that cattle may be encountered at any point, and it is that danger this Bill is intended to guard against. ' Can it be said that parliament has fairly and intelligently sought to protect the safety of the public, when during twelve or fourteen years, although there is a law on the statute-books requiring railways to provide cattle-guards and proper fences to keep cattle from going on their tracks, these companies have been allowed to systematically disregard that law, with the result that all over the country we have had disasters to cattle and the owners of the cattle have had to bear the loss ?
The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Thompson) has spoken out in a manner that does him credit. He spoke of the stand he was taking to have justice done our farming community, but judging from what passed last session I have not much hope for this measure should the course, which he recommends, be pursued this year. He

says we can go to a special committee and get tlie evidence. But what better evidence can we get than that of our senses ? What witnesses do we want to call 1 Is it not evident that if this is to be a short session and this Bill is referred to a committee, it will not get beyond that committee. Justice delayed, Mr. Speaker, is injustice, and surely .justice has been long enough delayed in this matter. If I understand the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) aright, he made a suggestion in the same line. He said that all parties interested could be heard before the committee. Well, I submit that all the parties interested can be heard when we deliberate the question in this House. What are we but the representatives, not alone of the farmers and the railway companies, but of the entire people of Canada; and the representatives of the people on the floor of this House can just as well, as honesty, and as faithfully represent the various interests concerned as could any witnesses before a committee.
I. think I am right in saying that although the two great parties in this Dominion have vied with each other in professing their readiness to protect the interests of the farmers, the discussion this afternoon has shown that some hou. members at least have not paid that attention to what is actually before the House in the agricultural interests which we would expect from their utterances on the public platform.
This point requires to be kept clearly in mind that the law which requires that cattle shall not be allowed to run at large within half a mile of the intersections of the railway track with the public highway, is not interfered with in any way by the proposed amendment of the hon. member for Lincoln. The courts have pointed out that the object of this provision was to make it in the interests of the farmers to keep their cattle at home. Under it if an animal is killed or injured, which has violated that section, the owner cannot recover damages, and hon. gentlemen may advance that as an argument against the amendment of the hon. member for Lincoln. I submit, however, that every argument which has been used by the legislature and the public to have the public interests safeguarded should be exerted in favour of this amendment. If we have truly the interests of the travelling public at heart, we should enact some measure similar to the one now before the House. Why so ? Because if you take the point of intersection between a highway and a railway alone, you will find that there is no temptation for cattle to loiter at that spot, though of course it is not impossible that an animal might by chance stray to that point and get caught there. But if that is possible, it would only happen at very long intervals. But when the law provides that the railway companies shall put up cattle-guards and fences along their lines sufficient to keep cattle
from straying on to the track and when we find this law completely disregarded-when we find a nice green sward along the railway lines offering tempting pastures to cattle-we have there not only a danger to the cattle but also a danger to the travelling public, which danger is vastly increased by practically allowing the railways to- dispense with cattle-guards at the points of intersection, since they are not liable to any penalty for accidents to animals occurring at these points.
The hon. member's amendment does not deal with the difficult question as to what kind of cattle-guards there should be, because that would lead to endless litigation and difficulty, but seeks a straight declaration that where cattle stray on to a railway track from the highway, by reason of the omission or neglect of the company to maintain cattle-guards or fences at the highway crossing, the company shall be responsible. The courts have decided that if an animal strays from the highway to the railway track, although there may be no cattle-guard or no fenee at the intersection between the highway and the railway, yet the owner of the animal must bear the loss, and we wish to make it the interest of the railway companies to guard against such accidents, which it is not their interest to do now. At present they insist on breaking the law by not putting up cattle-guards, simply because the courts have held that they are not responsible. Well, we can remedy that difficulty. We are all-powerful here. Do lion, gentlemen of the House of Commons think it fair that, because a farmer's cattle accidentally break out of their pasture during a wind storm, stray upon the highway and are thence tempted upon the railway and destroyed, it may be, a mile or a mile and half from the point of intersection, there shall be no compensation for the farmer ? Is it fair that by being given freedom from responsibility the railway company shall be tempted to disregard its plain duty ? If we say that the paramount consideration is the protection of railway passengers, I submit that it is in the interests of these very people that the proposition of the hon. member for Lincoln should pass. I submit also that it is not in the interests of the people that this Bill should go to a committee again, having regard to the experience we had last session.

speakeroldname: Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER (Mr. Peter Macdonald, East Huron).
speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
A large number of farmers throughout the length and breadth of this country have suffered heavy losses through the defective condition of the cattle-guards on railways. The old pit-guard was much more effective in preventing cattle wandering upon the railway than those that are now in use in some parts of the country. In fact, if the railway cattle-guards in other sections are built as they are in my riding then, there are no cattle-guards but

are absolutely useless. A number of my constituents have lost their valuable cattle and horses through there being, practically speaking no obstruction placed in the way of the animals wandering upon the track. The difficulty does not always arise, in fact it does not frequently arise, through cattle being driven along the highway and across the railway track. But, sometimes, as every hon. gentleman knows, cattle are pasturing in a field adjoining a side line. During a windy night the fence may blow down, or the cattle may find a panel which falls without much resistance, and thus they wander down the side line to the track. If it is in the middle of summer, and the feed is better on the railway than on the highway, as it often is, the cattle naturally wander along the railway and so are liable to be killed by passing trains. If there were efficient obstructions, the cattle would continue on the highway and would thus avoid danger. Let me quote one instance to show the absolute' uselessness for the purpose intended of the cattle-guards. One evening a number of cattle, owned by one of my con-stitutents about four miles from the town in which I live, broke down some fences and wandered down to the side line till they came to the crossing. The feed being better on the railway, they wandered upon the track. The train passed, I think in the night, and killed four head of cattle. The carcasses were thrown from the track to the side of the road. The owner had to take them from where they lay to bury them in another place. He hitched up his horse to a wagon and actually drove over the cattle-guard with his horse and wagon to the place where the carcasses were, and then drove back, without difficulty, over the cattle-guard. This shows that there was no obstruction thrown in the way of the cattle wandering on the railway. In this way, large numbers of cattle and horses are killed. Two other constituents of mine lost valuable horses in the same way, and still another lost three or four head of cattle. When we consider the number of valuable animals killed in this way, we see that this is an exceedingly serious and important question. It is for us to consider the best means to be adopted to secure better protection for the owners of cattle. I do not say that this Bill will accomplish all that is necessary; nor do I say that the railways are guilty of neglect. But, if proper cattle-guards cannot be constructed now, some railway men ought to apply their wits to the inventing of a cattle-guard which will prevent animals wandering on the railway. The old pit-guards were the ones in use in our neighbourhood some years ago. But all these guards have been filled up solid to the top, and a few longi-tudinous strips, triangular in form, have been placed where the pit formerly was. But sheep and cattle can pass over them without any difficulty whatever. It is Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER.
the duty of parliament to consider this question, not from a party standpoint-for there is no partyism in it-and do the best we can to secure safety for cattle and horses that wander on the highway through no fault of the owner. Whether it is considered in Committee of the Whole or in the Railway Committee matters not, if we do our duty. I rose merely to tell the House of the state of affairs in my own neighbourhood and to show the ineffectiveness of the cattle-guards in use there.

I understand, that this Bill, if enacted, would make the railway corporations liable for loss through cattle being killed on the railway track, if those cattle stray upon the railway from the highway. That being the case, I am thoroughly in sympathy with the Bill. I believe, that, if such a Bill were enacted, the railway companies would soon devise some means by which the cattle would be prevented from straying on the track from the highway, yet which would not interfere with them running a train. Some years ago, a law was passed prohibiting cattle roaming at large within half a mile of the railway track. Was that law passed in the interests of the farmers ? Was there any great demand on the part of the farmers for such a law ? If cattle got out and got on the railway track and were killed, farmers had no compensation before that law was passed and they have had no compensation since. The argument used at that time was that the law was necessary for the protection of railways as cattle going upon the track might be the means of derailing trains and so causing expense to the railway company. If that is the object to be attained, I think the railway companies should have no objection whatever to the Bill now before us. If there is danger of trains being derailed at the highway crossings by cattle going upon the track, that danger must be greatly increased, if the cattle go, as they do now, on the property of the railway, and are free to wander upon the track where they will. It would be in the interest of the railway, as it would be in the interest of the railway employees and of the general tra velling public, to pass such a law as is here proposed. If this law were passed, efficient cattle-guards would be provided, and danger of this kind would be restricted to the points where the railways and the highways cross.

I would not rise to discuss the merits of this Bill were it not that we may be called upon to vote as to whether the Bill should be sent to the Railway Committee or not. I am one of those who desire to weigh carefully the interests of the farmers as to how this Bill may affect them; but I am not blind to the fact that this country is an agricultural country, and that our railways may be more patronized by agriculturists
3i

than perhaps by any other class of the community. That being the case, while I recognize that the farmers located along the lines of railway may suffer to some extent through accidents caused by the railways. 1 also remember that the greater portiou of the agriculturists of this country are not located on a railway, but are travellers over railways; and we have to consider whether we may not do an injustice to the greater number of farmers by legislating so as to make our roadbeds perhaps insecure or unsafe to the travelling public, and by that means perhaps causing a greater sacrifice of life on our railways than takes place at present. Now, I remember that on the old organized railways of this country, they had the kind of cattle-guard that was built when the railways were first constructed, known as the pit cattle-guard. The hon. gentleman who moved this Bill to-day, throughout his speech, spoke as if that was the kind of cattle-guard he suggested, and the only difference is that he requires it to be constructed of masonry instead of square timber, as it had been by the old organized railways.
Now what has been the history of the railway companies with respect to cattle-guards, wooden culverts and wooden bridges in this country ? At first they were wooden culverts built across the railways; but the railway companies, finding they had to compete with those of the United States found it necessary to introduce engines of greater power and of greater speed in order to compete with American railways, and for that purpose they filled up the culverts, the cattle guards, and rebuilt their wooden bridges with iron. I remember distinctly, by practical experience, that the cattle-guards in those days did not prevent stock from passing on the railways, frequently stock was killed by passing over the cattle-guards on to the railways. When my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says that the railway companies do not care when stock passes over the railway, it is idle rot to talk like that. The hon. gentleman regretted very much that cattle were not allowed to run on the highway. Then my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) who, according to the ' Farmer's Sun,' has paid a great deal of attention to this Bill, and who ought to be prepared, if any man in this House can be, to enlighten us on the subject of this legislation, makes an erroneous statement. He says that cattle do not linger around the intersection of a railway crossing. Well, I want to tell my hon. friend as a practical railway man that if there is one place more than another where stock running at large are likely to linger, it is at the intersection of a railway crossing. There is no question about it, and every practical railway man will tell you so. Then again it has been suggested by one hon. member in this House that the
pit is a proper guard to have. The hon. gentleman has never had any experience ; he does not know.
I am prepared to say, perhaps having had as much experience in the matter as any other hon. gentleman in this House, that X am not in a position to say to-day that this Bill should be referred to a Committee of the Whole House. X have not the information in my possession which would justify me in voting against the Bill, or which would justify me in voting for it. But I do not want to leave myself open to the charge by any man who chooses to come into my constituency and tell the farming community that simply because I voted against this Bill being considered in Committee of the Whole I am therefore opposed to legislation of this character. I do not want to put myself in such a position, and I believe many other hon. gentlemen in this House wish to avoid putting themselves in that position. I go further, and say that railway companies in this country are just as eager as any hon. gentleman in this House to prevent loss of life on the railways and to prevent loss of stock to the farmers on the railways. Until we have an opportunity of sending for witnesses and securing statistics which would justify us in amending this legislation, I say it becomes us to go slowly. Now when this Bill was before the House last session there were no petitions asking us to pass this legislation. Since then a strong agitation has sprung up throughout the country, and many petitions have been sent to this parliament. Hon. gentlemen are well aware that the public are alive to this question. That being the case, is it not our duty, in the interest of the public and in the interest of all parties, carefully to weigh this question ? The only way we can do so is by securing statistics to ascertain whether more stock is killed in winter or more stock is killed in summer, and what are the causes of these accidents. My hon. friend from Huron said that stock may break out through fences. Why, Sir, will the hon. gentleman pretend to say that it is only when they break through fences that cattle get on railway crossings over the intersections with the highway ? That is rarely the case. Frequently in the dry season of summer the fences are burnt by reason of sparks from the engine setting the grass on fire along the railway, and frequently this allows the stock to get out on the railway. Will any one pretend to sav that you require a cattle-guard wherever cattle break out through the fences alongside the railway ? Certainly not. No legislation we can pass in this House will prevent accidents occurring on railways by reason of broken fences caused in the way I have described.
Now, farmers are interested in more ways than one in this question. They are interested as travellers and they are interest-

ed as owners of stock, and we ought to weigh these separate interests carefully. When my hon. friend, my colleague from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson), says that we are bound to consider the interest of the farmer, I say we are bound to consider his interests both as a traveller and as an owner of stock. I have just as much right to consider his interest as a traveller as I have to consider his interest as an owner of stock that may be killed through carelessness, or perhaps by accident. When this Bill comes up before the Railway Committee, if it ever does, I shall be glad to do my best to give it full consideration, and to procure information that will enable us to come to a right decision. I may add that if it comes to a question in this House as to whether we shall send this Bill to the Railway Committee, I have no hesitation in saying that I will support the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who has proposed to send it to that committee.

I have just one word to say as to the aspect which this debate has taken. No matter how much we may be in favour of the Bill of the hon. member for Lincoln, it now seems to me that each member of the Railway Committee who sits in this House must consider whether he is prepared to vote want of confidence in himself. The discussion has been going on and arguments have been advanced to show that we ought to consider this Bill in Committee of the Whole House because the Railway Committee would not treat it fairly. The man who takes that view must be prepared to support a resolution which says that the Railway Committee does not do its duty. Are we, members of this House who are members of that committee, going to stigmatize ourselves by voting that this Bill should be considered now because we will not give it proper consideration when it is sent before us in the Railway Committee in the ordinary course. That is the first proposition that presented itself to me, but these hon. gentlemen who think that it should be considered now as a safeguard to the farming community seem to forget, while perhaps they will be earning a certain amount of eclat before the pnb-lic by making it appear that they are protecting the interests of the public, that in future a fashion may be created which I am sure every hon. gentleman will condemn. If it is to be said that a Bill may be more easily put through in this way, shall we not have every day persons representing different interests in the community coming here and saying : This is a very important Bill; it will not receive proper consideration before the Railway Committee and therefore we want it considered now. I have always thought, and I think the members of this House will agree with me, that the more important a Bill is the more im-Mr. INGRAM.
portant it is that it should be sent to the Railway Committee in order that all the matters connected with it may be discussed and all views heard. Therefore, I am preprepared to support the resolution of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Sutherland), sending it to the Railway Committee, in order that we may have a full and free discussion there by the representatives of all parties, and further than that, I am not prepared to vote a want of confidence in myself as a member of that committee.

Mr. Speaker, it appears to me that there is no better place in which to thresh out this measure than right here in Committee of the Whole. This Bill has been before the Railway Committee on several former occasions. I remember that for four or five years back there is not a county in our section of the country that has not petitioned this government regarding cattle-guards. This is not a new thing, and I am of the opinion that every hon. member here, representing a county, is a good judge as to whether the county which he represents desires a change in the law relating to cattle-guards or not. It is not for us as members of the House of Commons to dictate to the railway companies as to what kind of cattle-guards they should adopt. I do not think they would pay any attention to us if we did dictate to them on this point. It seems to me that a cattle-guard should be sufficient to keep stock off the tracks. It is for the railway companies, in my opinion, to settle for themselves as to what sort of cattle-guards they should build, and not for us to dictate to them, provided that they adopt a safe cattle-guard. I was surprised at the speech of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes). He tried to make it appear that there was more danger to the travelling public by having a good cattle-guard to prevent cattle from getting on the track than by having a poor cattle-guard that would permit cattle to get on the track. That is his argument. There are four rods of the highway clear between the fences where cattle may get upon the railway track, but if there is an insufficient cattle-guard cattle might occupy the track for the two or three miles that intervenes between the two guards. I can only say that I have had the honour of being a member of the county council for some years and that every year they have petitioned this government asking for more protection in the shape of better cattle-guards.
Mr. Speaker, before this question is put, I desire to say a few more words in regard to this matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: He might speak in a discussion but not on the Orders of the Day.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. James Sutherland) moved that the Bill be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Railways and Canals and Telegraph Lines.

Mr. Speaker, before that motion is put, I desire to say a few words, and with all due respect to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Sutherland), to contend in this House that we are not doing- the right thing by sending this Bill to any committee other than the Committee of the Whole House. I have listened very earnestly and very carefully to all that has been said as to the reasons of hon. gentlemen for desiring this Bill to go to the Railway Committee, and I have been struck most forcibly by one thing. The hon. gentlemen who want this Bill to go to the Railway Committee, not always for the same reason, but for some reason or other, seem to have doubts as to whether the Bill is a proper one to pass-not putting it any stronger than that, not contending that the amendment which I have been seeking to bring into force is a bad one or one that should not be passed, and paying that compliment to those hon. gentlemen who have spoken in favour of the Bill, and who are not prepared to say that it is not a good measure, but at the same time there may be reasons which may come out in the Railway Committee. I have asked hon. gentlemen in this House to tell me whether the Railway Committee of this House is the body that is entrusted with the enactment of public laws or whether the whole House is the body that is so trusted by the people. I would ask hon. gentlemen like the hon. member from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), who says that he does not want to be placed in the position of voting against this Bill or voting for it in the House, to ask himself whether he did hot put himself in that position when he accepted the nomination and was elected to serve the people in parliament.

May I be permitted to answer the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) ? If this Bill is referred to the Railway Committee, the Railway Committee deals with it, and if this House is dissatisfied with the report of the Railway Committee, this House has the power to change it.

Then, I say, still speaking of the hon. member for East Elgin, that he is deputing to the Railway Committee the duty which was placed upon him and not upon the Railway Committee when he accepted a position of trust as a member of parliament. The members of the Railway Committee do not constitute all the members of the House of Commons. It is the duty of every member of the House of Commons to pass upon the general laws of the country and if they are going to pass upon the general laws they cannot properly pass upon them unless they have an opportunity of discussing them. Why should we exclude any member of the House of Commons from the discussion of a Bill relating to the general public laws of the Dominion ? The position that these hon. gentlemen place themselves in seems to me to be nothing else than that they are willing to have a committee of perhaps half the House of Commons-not exactly but perhaps not more than half-to pass upon a general matter that is to be discussed, upon all the details and then the members of the House of Commons who are not members of the Railway Committee are to come in upon the third reading of the Bill and ask themselves whether the judgment of the Railway Committee was right or wrong. How can they reasonably do so if they are not members of the Railway Committee ? Therefore, the members of the whole House of Commons must pass upon the Bill themselves and judge whether it is a right and proper law to pass. In regard to what was also said about the kind of cattle-guards, I have found out-perhaps every hon. member of the House has not-but they can easily find out that the people's railway, the railway the people undertake to operate, provides proper cattle-guards.
When we find on the Peoples' Railway, the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway-that proper cattle-guards are constructed, the other railway companies have a very poor case when they come to parliament to ask for any less liability to be placed upon them. During my trip through the maritime provinces last summer-which I flo not pretend to say I took solely for the purpose of investigating cattle-guards-I did not forget my duties to my constituency nor to the whole of Canada, so far as I have a duty to the whole of Canada, and I made particular inquiries as to the kind of cattle-guards on the Peoples' Railway and as to the effect of them. I was told by the trainmen on the Intercolonial Railway that they did not know of a case where a cow had been on that railway between the highway crossings. That I think disposes of the matter pretty effectively. These crossings where the highway and the railway intersect will have more or less cattle collected about them ; but the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has forgotten that the amendment I am seeking to incorporate in the law will prevent these cattle from being killed anywhere else but on the highway crossings, and will not permit of them getting anywhere else than on the part of the line which is both a railway and a highway. I shall not detain the House longer, but I do say to the minister (Hon. Mr. Sutherland)

DEMERS (St. John and Iberville) (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, The question now before us is not so complicated as has been contended by many of the hon. gentlemen who have taken part in the debate. What we have to decide is, whether we are going, by an amendment to allow the courts to alter their decisions. *We are asked to give by an amendment to the law, our sanction to a provision which is already on our statute book. Under these statutes railway companies have to erect cattle guards at railway crossings ; but through an amendment introduced in 1890, the law was changed and railway companies are no longer responsible before the courts when cattle are permitted to be at large upon any highway.
The question before us, is whether we are going to amend the law, and whether we are to allow the courts to condemn railway companies which do not comply with the law. That is the whole question in a nutshell. The question is not whether cattle guards are to be built , in such or such a way ; but whether a company which does not construct any such cattle guards or does build them in a defective way-which comes to the same thing-will be held liable for damages. Is it a question which requires to be submitted to the consideration of the railway committee ? By no means. It is a most simple question. I would have voted Mr. LANCASTER.
this year for the motion of the horn Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Sutherland) as I did last year, had I not been since educated upon all the quibbles and technicalities of parliamentary procedure. I wish to wash my hands of the whole affair, and I decline to assume any responsibility in connection with any change that the Act may have to undergo this year.

We draw the attention of Mr. Galibert to the bad state of the road, particularly between Montreal and La Longue Pointe.
The Turnpike Trust must not only collect tolls ; they are obliged also to keep in good condition the roads under their control. They have an inspector who must have forgotten to make his tour of inspection, and it is high time his attention were called to the complaints that are heard from the public. Now, the road between Montreal and La Longue Pointe is only a single track road and it is in an awful state. The public have a right, however, to insist upon a double track road and one that is properly maintained. We are sure Mr. Gaii-bert will give stringent orders to the inspector of the Turnpike Trust.
As I said a little while ago, the government who appoints the members of that com-mision and to whom there is due a very high amount on which no interest has been paid for many many years back, the government, I say, has a right to inquire thorougli-
