Let me tell you that presently no one has the right or if that right exists, we are prevented from exercising it, and no one, as I have said, is allowed to see what is going on.
My object, in moving for the return, is to give publicity to the affairs of that trust, to call the attention of the government to then-management, and after that to ask the ministers if they could not see their way clear to lighten the heavy burden under which the farming community is being crushed. The farmers in the counties of Terrebonne, L'Assomption, Two Mountains, Jacques Cartier and Laval, which latter county I have the honour to represent in this House, are obliged to pass twice a week through these toll-gates, where they have to pay a very high toll and also upon the bridges in the vicinity of Montreal. If a farmer crosses the toll-gate at half-past eleven at night he has to pay ten cents and he comes back after midnight, say forty minutes later, he is obliged to pay another ten cents. I was told by a farmer that he had paid $75 in tolls upon the bridges, and passing through the toll-gates.
The farmers in the vicinity of Montreal sell all their products on the markets of that city. They are not exporters and they also have the right-whether they sent here Conservative members or Liberal members- to ask the government to look into the management of the affairs of that trust composed of parties appointed by the Dominion and Provincial governments.
In concluding these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I hope that this government at the hands of whom the farmers of Canada have already received so much protection, will not be less generous to those residing around Montreal in the counties of Jacques Cartier, Laval, L'Assomption and Terrebonne, and that they will come to their assistance.
I move this motion, seconded by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk).
Are we going to get no statement from the government in regard to this matter ?

I thought my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) was going to address the House or otherwise I would have risen to say that so far as the motion is concerned there can be no objection to it. Any papers in the hands of the government or which can be reasonably obtained will be brought down. I think there is some misapprehension as to the position of the government in this matter. It will be readily understood that under ordinary circumstances it is not the business of the Dominion government to maintain roads in any part of the country. That is a municipal or provincial matter as the case may be. The only interest the gov-Mr. LEONARD.
eminent of Canada has in this is as the holders of certain bonds. If my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) is under the impression that the government is getting revenue from these bonds and thus oppressing the people,
I am able to assure him that he is mistaken. We hold these bonds in consequence of transactions of older times. Under an arrangement made some years ago, this debt was reduced and a basis of adjustment was reached which the government of the day were led to believe would enable the Turnpike trust to pay interest on the reduced sum. For a year or so some interest was paid but later on no interest was paid. Whether or not this is the fault of the commissioners is a proper subject for inquiry, and if any representations on that question are made it will be our duty to look into the matter very carefully. All I can at present say is, that the government are receiving no revenue. We have a large amount of Dominion money invested, and though a reduction was made some years ago in the hope of receiving some satisfactory settlement, we are not now receiving any interest. If that arises from the fault of the commissioners of course it is a matter for which the government should be called to account, but if it arises because the traffic is not large enough to maintain the road and pay the interest, I suppose it is like a good many bad debts and we shall have to make the best of it under the circumstances.

It is very easy to see that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) took no very active interest in the recent by-election which was held in the county so ably represented by my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard). But it is a little discouraging to us to see that the right hon. leader of the House, who came into the county, who knows what a deep interest we have in this question, who I think referred to it on nomination day-does not, now that the election is over, see fit to give us some assurance as to the things which his friends throughout the county during the election, pledged the government to accomplish. They were very sanguine during the election and they strongly urged the electors to vote for the opponent of my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) because he was the only one that could get from the government the action which was necessary to relieve the people of Laval and the adjoining counties. But the day of the election is over. We have the spectacle of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, not uttering a single word on this, to us, most important question, and we have the Minister of Finance informing us that the government derives no revenue from these bonds. I can tell my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) not only that the government derives no revenue from these bonds, but that they will never receive a cent of the capital. He ought to be aware of that fact, and not being aware of that fact,

it is the duty of the government to come to the relief of the farmers of the counties mentioned by my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) and to do something to put a stop to the abuses which exist there, and which are the fault of these gentlemen opposite to so large an extent. Mr. Speaker, although the question of the Montreal Turnpike Trust was much discussed during the last election, and although the right hon. prime minister referred to it at the meeting on nomination day eight days before the election, yet the government could not give us any satisfactory assurance that some redress would be granted for the grievances which formed the subject of continual debate during the election. Let me acquaint the members of this House as briefly as possible with the nature of those grievances, and the remedy which it is In the power of the Dominion government to provide for them.
The Montreal Turnpike Trust, which controls all the great avenues into the city of Montreal from the surrounding municipalities is an old corporation, an administrative body, organized at the beginning of the last century, and replete with those faults which characterized every administrative body in this country before the great municipal reforms took place which have brought about the changes which you see to-day in every other corporate body. Thus, to give you an example, although It is an administrative body, charged with the administration of the public roads around the city of Montreal, and consequently a body whose work and deliberations interest every citizen of Montreal and every farmer who has access to Montreal from the surrounding parishes, still the law declares that no outsider has a right to attend the deliberations of this body. Our municipal councils are open to the public, and every other public body holds its sessions in public. Here in this parliament modern progress has required that the public shall be admitted to our deliberations. But the Montreal Turnpike Trust is the only exception to that general rule that X know of in this country. In that sense and in every other sense it is a close corporation.
Another short-coming of that corporation, in regard to which the people of Laval and the people of my own constituency complain very bitterly, is that its work is not done in the way in which public works are now done throughout the country, that is, by tender and contract. The Montreal Turnpike Trust has yearly deficits. The roads around the city of Montreal, as is well known to all who have occasion to pass along them, 16*
are in a deplorable condition both summer and winter. My hon. friend from Laval has cited some of the utterances of the press of the city of Montreal in regard to those roads, and from year to year, since 1896, for some reason or other, these roads have been kept in worse and worse order every succeeding season, until this winter it has been a subject of comment, not only in the newspapers of Montreal, but in the whole surrounding country, that our winter roads under the administration of this Turnpike Trust are in a disgraceful condition. The work not being done by tender and contract, we do not get the worth of our money. The contracts are given to friends, to men who have agreeable relations with the members of the Trust, very often to incompetent men who sublet the work ; and the result is that for the large amount of money that is expended yearly on these roads we have not an adequate return. In that respect, again, the law requires to be altered, so that the trustees shall be required to solicit public tenders for all works of importance, and to give the contract to the lowest responsible tenderer.
Under the charter which governs that corporation it is impossible for those who are interested in the proper administration of the Trust to see how the money has been expended. Here, in Ottawa, the expenditures of the government are subject to strict scrutiny. We have a yearly audit, and we are fully acquainted with what is done with the money which goes into the public treasury. The same thing obtains in the different provinces, as well as in all the municipalities in our province, and I have no doubt everywhere else. The banks themselves, which in a certain sense are private corporations, give a yearly account of what is done with their funds. But there is no such law applicable to this corporation, and as a consequence one is obliged every year to move, here or in the provincial legislature, in order to obtain some idea of what lias been done with the very considerable revenue which this corporation derives from the taxpayers and from those who use the roads. That, again, was a point frequently adverted to in the last election, and candidates on both sides and their friends pledged themselves that they would insist, with this government as well as with the provincial government, that that great defect in the law should be cured, and that we should have yearly returns from this corporation in order that we might know how our funds are administered.
The consequence of the present system is that we have bad roads. This corporation controls all the great avenues into the city of Montreal, and their control goes so far that it prevents the proper development of the great suburban municipalities which surround the city. If any municipality or any private individual opens a road in order to facilitate access to the city for the public,

and that road happens to intersect one of the great avenues which are under the control of this body, what do they do ? They place a toll gate at the intersection, and the man who is merely crossing their road for the purpose of following some new municipal highway or some road which has been opened by a private individual who wishes to sell lots and thus increase the development of the city of Montreal, he has to pay toll to the Montreal Turnpike Trust. The result is that it checks the opening up of new roads which are rendered necessary by the subdivision into lots of farms surrounding the city and the building on those lots, and absolutely paralyses the development of the city of Montreal. If on that point the law were altered, and it were declared that the mere intersecting of one of the turnpike roads by some municipal or private road would not necessitate the payment of tolls, that would be some remedy for what is to-day a crying grievance. The Montreal Turnpike Trust, owing to this frequent intersecting of their roads, have been obliged to add very considerably to the number of their toll bars.
We have arrived at this result, that on a revenue of $60,000 or $65,000 a year from these toll gates, they are obliged to expend at present over $18,000 a year merely for the maintenance of these gates which, in the proper course of things and which with judicious legislation, could no doubt be made to disappear, as they have disappeared in the neighbourhood of every large city upon the continent of America.
The hon. the Minister of Finance has stated that this corporation was the creation of the provincial legislature, and that the government of the Dominion derived no revenue from the $200,000 of bonds which it held in this corporation and were powerless to interfere. Let me point out why it is considered in the counties of Jacques Cartier, Laval and the others surrounding Montreal, that the key of the situation is in the hands of the Dominion government. Under the law, this government, being a creditor of that corporation to the extent of over $200,000, is entitled to representation on the board of directors. There are, if I mistake not, three representatives of this government on that board, and they are the majority. The other two commissioners are appointed by the provincial government.

There are seven, if the hon. gentleman will allow me to correct him, and the provincial government has a majority.
Mr. MONIL My hon. friend is mistaken. There are five trustees in all-two named by the provincial government-which has created this body and to a certain extent controls it, which has the right to legislate with regard to it-and three named by the Dominion government, which is the only Mr. MONK.
creditor of the Montreal Turnpike Trust. The control is therefore in the hands of the Domionion government, and any legislation which the trustees named by the provincial government might wish to obtain in the Quebec legislature may be vetoed by the three trustees who represent the Dominion. And as a matter of fact, a year or two ago, when a member of the provincial legislature sought to obtain'by positive enactment a remedy to one of the numerous grievances which we complain of, he failed to succeed because the Dominion government, through the Minister of Finance, interfered to oppose that legislation and obtained its rejection upon the ground that the legislation proposed might have the effect of diminishing the* revenues of this Dominion, although I may say the interest on the bonds have not been paid since 1896, We claim therefore that the Dominion government, by its yearly election of these three commissioners, has the control of the Montreal Turnpike Trust and is the power behind the throne which can control legislation and obtain for us the reforms that are absolutely needed.
Let me tell you, Sir, what this question was which was agitated in the Quebec legislature. As my hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) knows-and I am glad to see he is taking an interest in this question and very sorry to see that the other members from the counties around the city of Montreal, who have an equal interest with myself in this important question, are not here to defend their rights-as my hon. friend from Gaspe knows, we have in the city of Montreal absolutely inadequate accommodation for our public markets. The farmers from the counties of Terrebonne, Two Mountains, Laval and from Ohambly, Laprairie and Jacques Cartier are, in consequence of that want of accommodation, obliged to leave their farms generally at eight or ten o'clock in the evening in order to secure some kind of a place upon the Bonsecour Market, the following day. Leaving their homes early in the evening, they pass the toll bars before midnight, and as they cannot return on the same day, midnight intervening, they are obliged to pay toll again on their return the following day. Under the Conservative rule that injustice was recognized, and the keeper of the toll-gate was authorized to issue tickets to the farmers, good for forty-eight hours. But no sooner had the trustees of my hon. friend the Minister of Finanee entered upon the board than that permission was revoked, and the member of my own constituency, who represents me in the local legislature, endeavoured to obtain the passage of a law obliging the Montreal Turnpike Trust to give to farmers tickets good for forty-eight hours. Thanks to the interference of the Dominion government that measure was blocked, and our farmers to-day, on account of the failure of the city of Mont-

real to give them adequate accommodation upon the central market, have been since 1896 obliged to pay double toll. It would be very easy to remedy that state of things. It could be done either by the passage of a law or by the Montreal Turnpike commissioners passing an ordinance or a by-law to make the toll five cents going and five cents returning. But this government appears to be so completely oblivious of the interests of the farmers and so forgetful of the pledges made by its partisans during the last election, that nothing whatever is done to remedy this injustice. What we want has been indicated by the hon. member from Laval. And it is in the power of this government very easily to obtain for the people what they want and give them satisfaction. We want public sessions of the Turnpike Commissioners. The body has not a representative character, but it should have that character. The mayors of the parishes in the counties interested ought to have the right, not by claiming permission, but the right by law, to go to the sessions of the Montreal Turnpike Trust, to witness what takes place there and to make necessary suggestions. It is for this government to determine whether it will use its influence in order to obtain them that right. The fact is that the body is not constituted as it should be. A body that is entrusted with the administration of such important interests as the proper keeping of the roads in the vicinity of Montreal, should have a representative character. The men who administer the great avenues approaching the city of Montreal should be elected. That is our contention; and a system could easily be devised, if these hon. gentlemen would only show us a little good will, by which, if not the whole body, at least a part of it, would be elected. The people would then feel that they have on that board somebody chosen by themselves to look after their interests in regard to these roads, which are so very important to them. Farmers generally come in three or four times a week from their homes to the city of Montreal, bringing heavy loads of their produce; and it is positively disgraceful to see the way in which the roads by which they must travel are now kept. Not only should we have representatives of the people in these bodies, but the sessions of the body should be made public. And we should have yearly returns of the financial operations of the Montreal Turnpike Trust, in order that we may see exactly what is done with oar money. We should have the power which is demanded by everybody upon the Island of Montreal-the power to intersect these great public highways with our municipal roads, our private roads-all roads opened in order to facilitate the development of that great city without being witnesses of such atrocious abuses as we see at present, the Montreal Turnpike Trust placing a toll-gate at the intersection
of these roads and charging every one full toll for simply crossing their road. That is a crying injustice, and it can be removed by legislation.
My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) does not mean that we have the power to legislate on the matter in this parliament ?

The Dominion government, in making its yearly election of three trustees, can impose upon these trustees-who control the body-any conditions it chooses. If, when that election takes plaee, and it takes place every year, the trustees named by my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding), for it is he himself who names them by sending down, I think, the Deputy Minister of Finance, to cast the annual vote, though it is to be cast in favour of these trustees-can give them any instructions necessary. He can instruct them that these reforms must be brought about by legislation. And, Mr. Speaker, we should have the forty-eight-hour ticket restored to us. My hon. friend from Laval knows how that question, small as it may appear to my colleagues here, was discussed during the last election. He pledged himself that, the first time he opened his lips in parliament, it would be to demand from the government the redress of these grievances. He has carried out his pledge; and now it is for members of the government and their friends who gave similar pledges during the election, to show similar sincerity by advocating-and seeing to it that what they advocate is carried out-a complete reform of the system. What is preventing progress is that the Dominion government is a creditor to that trust to the enormous sum of, I think, about $200,000. I have told the House before, and the hon. Minister of Finance admitted it last session, that the existence of that great claim obliged him to oppose the passage of salutary legislation in the provincial legislature. What I suggested last year to the Minister of Finance, and what I suggest again, is this : There is no doubt whatever that not one cent of that indebtedness will ever be discharged. My hon. friend from Gasp6 (Mr. Lemieux) knows perfectly well that, with the increasing wants of the trustees in order to maintain the roads in good order, with the yearly increase of the charge to maintain toll-gates multiplying them every year, it is impossible to conceive any circumstances under which any part of that capital will be repaid. The House knows that, since 1896, not one cent of the interest has been paid. And the hon. Minister of Finance, if he takes the trouble to inquire, will receive ample assurance that the trust will never be able to pay one single copper of the interest. Under these circumstances, I suggested last year, and I suggest again to the government, that it should intimate to the local legislature, which has the power to legislate, and also to the trustees, the ma-

jority of whom are the nominees of this very government that, as soon as the grievances of which the counties that I have already named complain, and complain with justice, shall have been removed by legislation, the government will be ready to forego its claim of $200,000-that claim being, as I have said, absolutely irrecoverable. And I venture to say here, without fear of contradiction from anybody who is acquainted with the subject, that on the day that that assurance has been given, and given in such a way as to insure the promise being carried out, the legislature of Quebec will have no more pressing matter before it than the reform of these abuses and the placing of the Montreal Turnpike Trust upon a reasonable basis, so that the rights of those who pay may be respected, as they ought to be. Let the government announce that as its policy. Let the government say to the trust that the remission of the debt is assured, if legislation approved of by this government is passed by the local authorities, and within a year of this date that vexed question-which, so long as it remains a question, will be agitated in every single election in the county- will be satisfactorily settled.

This debate, so far as it has gone, will serve to illustrate once more the wisdom of the rule which requires that, when a demand is made for papers, the speech in support of the motion ought to be limited to merely describing what is required, and the debate on the main question ought to be deferred until such time as the House is placed in possession of the documents. Now, what are we called upon to deal with here? We are called upon to deal with the affairs of a corporation which is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the local legislature of Quebec. After having listened to my hon. friend, Mr. Speaker, you would naturally be under the impression that this is a very substantial grievance that he has made known to the House to-night.
Now listen to the other side of this case. I have to admit that I am going to speak with imperfect information at my disposal, because this is not a matter that one looks after in advance of the production of the documents. My hon. friend says that in the county of Laval, the county of Jacques Cartier, and other counties in the vicinity of Montreal, they have very bad roads, and that because they have very bad roads this government ought to be brought to task for it. Now, Mr. Speaker, in the vicinity of every great city in this country all the rural municipalities should have roads, they are a necessary adjunct of our civilization, you cannot get on without them. But how are these roads created ? How are they maintained ? These roads are created by the municipalities for the uses of which they are intended, and they are maintained by these municipalities.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: What did my hon. friend tell you ? He says these roads we now speak of were created by the expenditure of the public money of Canada, of the old provinces of Canada. They never cost the inhabitants one farthing, and still we don't maintain them after having created them. That is their grievance.
We pay for their maintenance.

Let me describe how they pay for them. These roads cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. At the present time the balance of capital, with the reduction that has been made in connection with the advances made on that portion which belongs to the Dominion of Canada, they still owe us. They cannot pay any interest even, there is $25,000 of accumulated interest on that indebtedness. Now if the ordinary business rule were applied by a government to a corporation indebted in the amount that I have described, they would first take care to see that the interest was paid.
What are they doing with the toll money for the roads ? Are the roads so bad they are not paying any interest on their bonds ?

The toll money does not produce enough to maintain the roads and pay interest on the bonds. But the ordinance under which the money was expended provides that the riparian proprietor, the man whose property fronts on that road, should contribute his share to the construction of that road, and they have never done it.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. I do not think he can cite that.

I have not prepared a special brief for this case to-night, but as my hon. friend has done so, I refer him to the ordinance, I think 4th Victoria, that created the trust, and he will find in that ordinance the ordinary common sense rule that the riparian proprietor, the man whose property fronts on this road, should contribute to its maintenance.
That is not what the section says.
Please allow me. I have not prepared a brief, but I have had some experience in legislation in this country.
But I think it is only fair that I should deny it.

The hon. gentleman has a perfect right to make a denial. As I said, I am speaking from recollection, and my hon. friend has a prepared brief, and on a prepared brief he takes the responsibility of making the denial, and he should accept that responsibility.	-

My hon. friend will allow me. We liave no rights whatever in these roads, the roads themselves belong to the Montreal Turnpike commissioners, and the riparian proprietor is not, under the law as it stands to-day, obliged to do any work on the roads.

He is not obliged to maintain the road at all. But here is what the law of the province of Quebec, says that the riparian proprietor is primarily responsible for the maintenance of the road that passes across his property. That is the general rule, and when this ordinance 4th Victoria was passed it was the rule then, and in order to meet that case and to provide that the riparian proprietor should not be relieved of his common law obligation to maintain his front, it is provided that the commissioners shall have the right to ask from the man whose property fronts on the road to commute his obligation to maintain the road, and to pay a sum equivalent to that obligation to the trustees.
That is what I said. That is a very different thing. Has that been done '!

That has not been done. My hon. friend had better remember that others have read the statutes besides himself. That is a statement I make, and he agrees with it. That has not been done, and if he wants these roads maintained let the riparian proprietors fulfil their legal obligation and they can easily maintain them.
I am glad to get that declaration from the government.

My hon. friend must bear in mind that in this case there are two parties to the dispute, there is the party of the proprietors in this part of the country that do not want to maintain their roads; there is the other side of the case, the ratepayers of the Dominion of Canada. The Dominion of Canada are creditors of these individuals, and we come to them and say :	If you cannot pay us the
capital at least pay us our interest.
But they do not.
But you did get something from them.
We got the interest, and we never got anything since. They paid the toll, but we didn't get any money.

My hon. friend says they got interest at the time.
I think if my hon. friend were to do as I asked him to do a minute ago, wait until the papers are brought down before expressing an opinion on this matter and he would find that the interest was not paid in those days, he would find that it was necessary that the capital should remain as it was, and the interest had accumulated to such an extent, and the burden had grown so large, that it was obligatory upon the government to reduce their claim even in those days, cut it practically in two, as the Minister of Finance tells me ; and notwithstanding that the claim has been cut in two, we are still asked to wipe out the balance of it. Now it does seem to me that we cannot very well afford to be so generous at the expense of the people of Canada. Besides, if we are going to do it for these people why not do it for my county ? Why not do it for all the rural municipalities represented here to-night ? Why should there be any distinction between them ? It seems to me that when in other parts of this country the ratepayers maintain their own roads, create and maintain them, these gentlemen should do likewise.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You did not give them a chance to take off the tolls.
Take off the tolls and give them the roads. Take off the tolls, and what is going to become of our capital and interest 1
What good is it now ?

If my hon. friend had ever gone through those municipalities he would have found out what it is good for. If he had ever seen the roads which have been created by which these gentlemen have benefited all these years, he would realize that the ratepayers in those municipalities are as well able and better able to pay than the ratepayers of nine-tenths of the municipalities in the Dominion of Canada.
How did it come about that the Dominion of Canada built roads in that particular portion of Canada ? It cannot be done in any other province.

Under the ordinance 4th Victoria, so far as my memory serves me-that was about 1840-two trusts were created, one in the vicinity of Quebec and the other in the vicinity of Montreal. These two trusts were created for the purpose of building roads in the neighbourhood of these cities. The trusts were unable to get the money necessary by the sale of debentures for the building of these roads. The debentures were offered to the public and the public lost what they put into the roads. The government took the balance. At the time of confederation these debentures that were held by the old province of Canada formed part of the assets of the Dominion and were distributed, one portion to what are now Ontario and Quebec, while another portion was assigned to the Dominion of Canada.
And the government guaranteed the interest.

Yes, the government guaranteed the interest and paid interest, but that was not on these debentures. The issue now is as to whether the persons who benefited by the construction of these roads, that is to say, the riparian owners, are under an obligation to pay for the construction of these roads, which they have not done. My statement is that under the statute there is what they call a commutation clause ; that is, that the riparian proprietor commutes his obligation to maintain his front into a money payment and that money payment has not been made.
I understand the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) to say that there is an obligation on the part of the riparian proprietor to maintain the road ?
There is an obligation made expressly by law upon him to pay his commutation money, and he ought to be made to pay it.
He had that to pay besides the tolls on the road.

Yes. The thing is very simple; a man, or a farmer, for Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
instance, might not have occasion to cross the toll bar; yet he has the use of the road and does not pay for it. Is that fair play, or justice, or common sense ?
Who is at fault for not collecting this commutation money ?
I consider the fault is on those who have allowed the commissioners all these years to go on without collecting it.
Were they the municipalities, or who were they ?
No, the commissioners themselves. They ought to be made to pay it.
It is the government not the commissioners.

Mr. Speaker, this question of the Turnpike Trust is nothing but an election cry, so much so that when the Tory government was in power the Liberals, in the county of Laval, agitated the question. In 1S88, Mr. Justice Fortin, the exmember of the county of Laval, was a candidate for the local legislature. The main plank of his platform was this very question of the abolition of the Turnpike Trust. In 1890 he was again a candidate in that county. He was then opposed by the Hon. Mr. Leblanc, one of the friends of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk), one of the most prominent Conservatives in Quebec, who stood by the Turnpike Trust, and who, speaking in Laval, to my recollection, said that the Federal government would never consent to remit the amount of $200,000 that was due. Now things have changed. We are on this side and my hon. friend is on the other side. He is asking this government to remit to the trust the sum of $195,000, because this is the amount due to the Federal government. I may say at once that the government has already been very generous, because some years ago the debt amounted to $400,000, and the then government remitted $200,000.
We will be satisfied if you do the same thing now.

It was then agreed that this amount was remitted in order to give the Turnpike Trust a chance to at least pay the interest on the balance; that is to say, on the sum of $200,000. They paid the interest for a few months, or a year or so, but later on we learned that the interest had been taken out of the capital. To-day the arrears of interest amount to $28,000. Now, I am very glad that this question has been brought up before the House by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, because, during the last campaign in Laval, where, fortunately for himself, he was successful where he placed a feather in his cap, my learned friend discussed that question on every hustings, but he has not given the government the benefit of his wisdom, he

has not told the government what was the remedy for the situation created by the Turnpike Trust in the surroundings of Montreal. He now prays the government to remit $195,000. But what will happen after that ? There are some other interested parties. The local government of Quebec is also a creditor, and there are some private individuals who are creditors. Shall they remit the amount or shall only the Federal government remit $195,000, and will the Turnpike trust do better than it has done in the past ?
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) allow me to ask him, what the indebtedness of the local government Is ?

I am not positive as to that, but I know the local government is also a creditor, because the local government has had two representatives, or two trustees, on the commission. Suppose the Federal government remits that amount of $195,000, what will happen ? Will the roads be kept in a better state, because, I understand, that this is the main issue this evening ? My learned friend bases his complaint on the deplorable condition of the roads in the surroundings of Montreal. What will happen if the government remits this amount ? Will the other interested parties do likewise and will the roads be repaired and maintained by the municipalities ? Will the municipalities of the county of Jacques Cartier and the county of Laval, represented by my two hon. friends, take upon themselves to maintain these roads ? I would be very glad to have a declaration from my learned friend because if he would return to his electors at the next election with this result, I do not think he would get their votes as he got them last time. If this amount were remitted by the local government and by the other interested parties and by the Federal government, the roads would have to be maintained by the municipalities. Therefore, I contend that this is not the place to discuss this question. It belongs to the local government, or the local legislature of Quebec. and it falls within the purview of the Municipal Code.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that I live far enough away from the turnpike road to enable me to say that I am not interested in the tolls. What strikes me in this discussion is that the government of the day are acting, not as private individuals would act. There is a debt owed by a certain trust. If the trust is able to pay, it is the duty of the government to enforce it, not to enforce it perhaps with all the severity of the penalties that a private individual would enforce a debt, but if the people are able to pay they should pay. We must not go back to ancient his-tor and say that because the Conservative government in the past did not collect this money when it might have collected it, this government should not collect it. What
has struck me in this discussion is that the question of this turnpike road and the remission or collection of the debt due has been used by the government as a political lever in every election. Surely this is a wrong thing on general principles for a government to enter into. I gather from the discussion that the right hon. Prime Minister of this country was one of those who took part in this election. I gather the question of the remission or collection of this debt was the subject of discussion between the different candidates. The supporters of the government candidate, among them the Prime Minister, let it be understood that if the electors should return their man the government would favourably consider the remission of this tax. That argument was used against the Conservative candidate. Well, fortunately for the county, Mr. Leonard, the Conservative candidate, was elected, and now evidently the government is going to do nothing. The Minister of Finance led the House to believe very squarely that this was one of the bad debts of the Dominion.
I did not say that.
Not directly, but I think you led us to infer it. You said that this would be probably like many others of bad debts and that it might be wiped out.
I said that under certain conditions it might be a bad debt.

I inferred from what you said that you looked upon this as one of the bad debts of the Dominion and from the discussion which I have heard up to that time, I agreed with you. But it would appear now that probably this debt is collectable, and if it is collectable it is the duty of the government to collect it. If it is not collectable it is the duty of the government to make as fair an arrangement as possible and wipe it off and get rid of it.
Do we always wipe off a debt because we cannot at once collect it ?
You do not, but some gentlemen say that the proprietors can pay it and then the government should force them to pay it.
My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) would not like that.

Do not let us have all this discussion about a debt that is owed by a municipality to this government and do not let us have it as a sore point for years and years, and made a factor in every election that may take place. If it is a bad debt, wipe it off; if it is a collectable debt, collect It.

In reply to some of the remarks made, I refer the

House to 3 Vie., chap. 31, paragraph 15, which provides :
And be it further ordained and enacted by the authority aforesaid, that from and after the passing of this ordinance, each and every person and persons, body or bodies politic or corporate,
who may be bound by any law of this province, or any procSs verbal duly homologated, (and all such laws and procgs verbaux, shall remain in full force, except in so far as they are hereby expressly derogated from) to repair or keep up, or to perform any service or labour, on or with regard to any portion of any road hereby placed under the control of the said trustees, shall and are hereby re paired to commute all such obligations with the said trustees for such sum of money as may be agreed upon by such parties respectively, and the said trustees, and such commutation money shall be payable annually, on the first day of March in each year.
And they have never paid a farthing.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: JUDGMENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL RE ROY VS. THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
JUDGMENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL RE ROY VS. THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext:
(Translation) moves for :
An address to His Excellency the Governor General for a copy of the report from the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, dated December 8, 1901, in the matter of an appeal from the Court of King's Bench for the province of Quebec (appeal side) between the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, appellant, and Adrien Roy, respondent.
It is not my intention to go at any great length into a review of the facts relating to the motion I have just put before the House. Let me say, at the very outset, that I am happy to see the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) in his seat, at a moment when I wish to call his attention to the disastrous consequences to the province of Quebec resulting from the recent decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council of England.
The hon. minister will, no doubt, realise the importance attaching to my motion, the more so as, more than any one else, he is able to represent here and voice the feeling of the province of Quebec, in so far as her laws are concerned. It is hardly necessary for me to remark that the hon. gentleman not only occupies a high standing among the members of the Bar of Quebec, hut that his high legal reputation is acknowledged even beyond this wide Dominion of ours. As I remarked before, the hon. minister, I am sure, will realize the importance of the issue I am now bringing before the House.
The judgment of the Privy Council just referred to has caused a painful sensation throughout the province of Quebec. Let me briefly sketch out the controversy in question. In 1899, a settler, by the name of Adrien Roy, living in one of the townships to the north of Montreal, being the owner Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
of a small timber limit, was the victim of a fire communicated to his property from the sparks of a locomotive belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Grounding his claim upon the law of our province and the jurisprudence sanctioned by our tribunals, he brought an action against the company, to recover the indemnity to which he was entitled. The case was heard before the Superior Court, presided over by one of our most eminent judges, Mr. Justice Langelier. After protracted pleadings, the company was sentenced, on December 5th, 1899, to pay to the defendant, as compensation, the sum of $300. Powerful as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is, it appealed from that judgment to the Court of King's Bench, presided over by five judges. The pleadings before that court were as protracted and as exhaustive as those that took place before the Superior Court. The Court of Appeal, without a dissentient voice, confirmed the judgment of the lower court.
As I said a little while ago, the amount of the litigation was but three hundred dollars, and under the Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, there could be no appeal to a higher tribunal. Let the House here allow me to call its attention to what in my view, is a most vicious practice, adopted by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Under the provisions of the code of civil procedure, the right of appeal is determined by the amount in litigation, or by contingent future rights. The code provides that there can be no appeal to the Privy Council of England, in cases where the amount at stake is under $2,000. But, in virtue of what may be called au ' appeal of grace,' the Privy Council sometimes allows litigants to be heard, even when the amount in litigation is below that sum. Such was the case in this instance, notwithstanding the formal prohibition enacted by the code. Therefore, the company, after ruining a poor settler, was condemned by our tribunals, but taking advantage of the privilege granted by the Lords of the Privy Council, they lodged a new appeal and succeeded in getting the unfortunate judgment I have just referred to, which reversed the whole jurisprudence sanctioned by a long series of decisions rendered by all the courts of the province of Quebec.
The Privy Council declared that, from the moment that a company was authorized by an Act of Parliament to run a railway, it could not be held liable for damages caused, when acting within the rights conferred by its charter.
The hon. gentleman will perhaps hear with surprise that such a doctrine was propounded by the Privy Council ; but, to clear up all doubts, let me quote from the ' dictum '-for there are no grounds whatever to be found in the judgment-of the Lord Chancellor of the Judicial Committee :-

But the ground upon which the immunity of a railway company for injury caused by the normal use of their line is based is that the legislature, which is supreme, has authorized the particular thing 30 done in the place and by the means contemplated by the legislature, and that cannot constitute an actionable wrong in England any more than it can constitute a fault by thy Quebec code.
And further on :
And the whole case turns not upon what was the common law of either,country, but what is the true construction of plain words authorizing the doing of che very .hiiig complained of. The legislature is supreme, and if it has enacted that a thing is lawful, such a thing cannot be a fault or an actionable wrong.
As I said, a railway company, which is empowered under a charter granted by the Dominion Parliament, to operate a railway, cannot be held responsible for damages caused, when acting within the rights conferred by its charter ; because, as they say, the legislature is supreme, which did confer such exorbitant rights.
This doctrine, astounding as it is, may be conformable to English law ; but though it may prevail in the old country, let it be remarked that, after this judgment had been rendered, the London ' Times,' the most important organ of public opinion in the empire, denounced the very next day that doctrine, and suggested that it should be given up, as contrary to equity. Let me further say this, that quite recently, Mr. Jeffries, member for Basingstoke, brought down a Bill for making railway companies liable for fires caused by sparks from their locomotives. The Bill has reached its second reading; the principle of it has been approved of by a large majority of the House of Commons; and if it has not yet reached its third reading, it is owing to the fact that parliament was prorogued. The Bill will come up again at the next session of parliament.
But supposing such doctrine prevailed in England, could the Lords of the Privy Council plead ignorance of the fact that in the province of Quebec, corporate bodies are assimilated by law to individuals. Article 1053 of the Civil Code reads as follows :
Every person capable of discerning right from w'rong is responsible for the damage caused by his fault to another, whether by positive act, imprudence, neglect or want of 3kill. Article 356 enacts, among other things :
Civil corporations constituting, by the fact ol their incorporation, ideal or artificial persons, are as such governed by the laws affecting individuals ; saving the privileges they enjoy and the disabilities they are subjected to.
So positive, so clear a text has never yet given rise to ambiguity before our tribunals. Moreover, our jurisprudence on that point has received the sanction even of the Supreme Court of Canada, the decisions of which, as a rule, are far from evincing any sympathy with our province.
In the case of Gareau vs. The Montreal Street Railway Company, Hon. Judge Girouard, of the Supreme Court, has given an opinion which tallies with the opinion of the Court of Appeal.
With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I shall quote from the judgment of the Court of Appeal, passing under silence the views expressed by Sir Alexander Lacoste, and by Judges Boss5 and Blanchet, who are of French extraction. But what did Judge Hall say ? X experience all the more pleasure in quoting his opinion, as he is, as shown by his name, of British origin. But it is a well known fact that he is a warm admirer of the French laws of our province. Listen to what the honourable judge says : The courts of this province have by a long series of decisions maintained the principle of responsibility for damage to a neighbour's property. Independently of the question of fault or negligence in the ordinary use of those words as well in cases of damage from flres set for clearing lauds, as by sparks from chimneys of industrial establishments.
The hon. judge then goes on quoting a long list of judgments, and says :
Whatever our personal opinion might have been upon the question we would certainly have felt controlled by the well set jurisprudence of our provincial courts, but we may add that wc entirely concur in the wisdom and equity of the rule which our courts have established. It is plain too, that in countries where a contrary rule is in force, many judges protest against its correctness and evade its effects where an opportunity presents. For instance, in Powell vs. Fall, in the Queen's Bench in England, the owner of a fraction engine in use upon a highway, under the authority of the English locomotive Act, and constructed in strict compliance with the terms of that Act, were held liable for damage caused by sparks setting Are to an adjacent stack, and Justice Branswell, In delivering the judgment of the court, remarked that the arguments of appellant council had been ingenious, but that he need only say in reply, that they had hardened his conviction that Rex vs. Pease and Vaughan vs. Taff Vale Company were wrongly decided.
Such was, in the eyes of Mr. Justice Hall, the jurisprudence established by our own tribunals and such was also the jurisprudence which even in England will before long prevail. Therefore, corporations, in the matter of liability for damages, are governed by the provisions of the Civil Code, and not as the Lords of the Privy Council unhesitatingly declared, by English common law. Such a construction constitutes, to our mind, a violation of the spirit and letter of our law. A jurisprudence, so well set for many years, they have ignored. No wonder, then, that such a deplorable decision should have come as a shock to us. For, let it be well understood, patient as we have been in the past of encroachments by the Dominion Government, we, from the province of Quebec, strong partisans as we are of provincial autonomy, shall not allow the Imperial authorities to infringe upon our rights, without loudly protesting. Of all things which we hold dear and sacred, and

which we wish to bequeath unimpaired to our posterity, we prize above all our civil laws and the French law, the existence of which was guaranteed to us by the constitution. So, scarcely had the judgment of the Privy Council been published, when it was most severely criticised and commented upon by the most eminent jurisconsults of our province. On January 7th, there appeared in the Montreal ' Gazette,' an article on the question, signed by ' Lex.' If I am rightly informed, ' Lex ' is no other personage than an English speaking judge, who is very well known in Montreal. Let me quote from that correspondence a few lines which need no comment:
To us, it appears that our law (as held by our courts) takes the only sensible logical position. Because the legislature grants a liberty to build and run a railway, it does not follow that the latter may set fire to my property and cause me damage without compensation. The law allows the road to run-so I, a proprietor on the line, cannot stop the running ; cannot obtain an injunction, although I may have well grounded fears of danger from fire. On the other hand the company can protect itself by adopting all the appliances which ingenuity can supply ; and by insuring against any loss which may occur.
' I say that our law so holds, rather it did so hold before the decision of the Privy Council above adverted to. In consequence of this decision, we shall nowr require the same legislation as they are asking for in England. They to get rid of their law as held by the courts, we, to get back to our law as our courts have held it to be.'
Another correspondent, who is one of the most eminent English speaking members of the Montreal Bar, writes as follows, to the ' Gazette,' in its issue of January 6th :
The judgment in Roy's case just rendered by the Privy Council strikes at the security, not only of every man's property, in this province within reach of fire from railway, but of every man's property that may be injured or burned by the operations of bodies carrying on any business authorized by their charters.
If railway companies, as their lordships hold, may with immunity burn people's properties along their lines, if they only use the latest fire screens, all other corporate bodies doing what they are authorized by their charters to do, are equally exempt from liability for their acts in destroying neighbouring properties.
It would be surprising if an effort is not made without delay, to place our law beyond question on this important subject, by legislation conformable to what our laws has always been as administered by our courts, and which every one feels is displaced by the Roy judgment in favour of a technical and inequitable rule of English law.'
If that judgment was severely commented upon by our English-speaking fellow-countrymen, I hesitate not to say that, among the French-speaking element, public opinion was thoroughly aroused. Hear what the 'Presse' has to say in an article which clearly betrays its trade-mark :
We have, so far, refrained from making any comment upon the judgment of the Privy Coun-Mr. LEMIEUX.
cil re Roy vs. the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, before having before us the text itself, but now that our doubts are cleared up, it is our duty to speak our mind, and to tell the public the unvarnished truth. We had until now, deluded ourselves into the belief that the craze for imperialism would at least show due respect to that last bulwark of political justice and equity, our courts of justice ; but we were mistaken.
That the Privy Council Lords have undertaken to make jurisprudence uniform as to a point wherein colonial jurisprudence is at variance with Engiish law, cannot be questioned. The noble Lords who have rendered this decision can hardly realise to what an extent they have injured their cause. They have just created a prejudice against an institution the real tendencies of which none ever dreamed to suspect, that it will take years and years to eradicate from the public mind. We had, so far, cheerfully accepted the decisions of the Privy Council, from a conviction that those judgments were rendered for Canada only and from the standpoint of our legislation but, now that the Privy Couacil seems to be promoted by a different feeling ; now that their judgments are framed in the light of a different legislation, it is quite another matter ; and an agitation is being, at this very moment, started into life, with a view to bringing about a change in the old procedure and for restricting those appeals, and, if need be, doing away with them altogether. Our legislatures have before them a heavy task.
I have said enough, Mr. Speaker, to show that this judgment of the Privy Council clearly inflicts a crying wrong upon the citizens of the province of Quebec who live under the authority of the Civil Code. That decision is a direct violation of our law, which nothing can atone for.
I make this motion in the hope that the lion. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) will see to it that the laws of this country are judiciously enforced.
The hon. Minister of Justice, now that he knows this decision, has a noble task before him. Let him amend, if need be, the Railway Act, and in drafting its clauses, let him use so clear a phraseology, that in the future, the Lords of the Privy Council may not be tempted into forgetting in this matter of responsibility and liability for damages, in fact that those great corporations are subject to the civil laws of the province of Quebec.
. We are happy to belong to the empire ; but any imperialistic scheme tending to* interfere with our rights and customs will And in us most irreconcilable opponents.

subtopic: JUDGMENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL RE ROY VS. THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: The report to which my hon. friend draws our attention is not one which is under the control of this House. It is a judgment rendered in a case between two private parties by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and is of course absolutely beyond our jurisdiction. No doubt my hon. friend knew this and made his motion simply for the purpose of criticising this judgment, and I am not here under any obligation to justify it at all.

subtopic: JUDGMENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL RE ROY VS. THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: JUDGMENT OF THE PRIVY COUNCIL RE ROY VS. THE CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY.
speechtext: I have no right to do it. I think it would be extremely unseemly on my part to justify or approve of a judgment rendered by their lordships of the Judicial Committee. However, I must say that, in all fairness, we should present that judgment as it really was rendered. It is possible so far as the province of Quebec is concerned, that previous to this judgment our impression was that our law differed somewhat from what their lordships have fouud it to be. What did their lordships decide ? They decided that the law in the province of Quebec, as we have it in our Civil Code, had been wrongly interpreted up to that time by our courts. Their lordships' finding may be good or bad, but they are the highest court in the land and we have to take the law as they construe it. The Courts of Appeal are for the purpose, of interpreting the law, and this, the highest court of appeal, has con-trued the law to be as I have said, namely, that in the province of Quebec the law applicable to cases, such as the one in question, is the same as it is in England and in the English provinces. What was the case ? It was one between an individual and a corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, created by the federal parliament, authorized by the federal parliament to carry on its operations throughout the whole of Canada, and running its railway through a portion of the province of Quebec. Under the sanction of the Dominion parliament this corporation operates that railway and in all respects conforms to the requirements of the statute which brought it into existence. Having in all respects complied with the law, an accident happened and fire was communicated from the railway to a barn in its vicinity. The Privy Council held that there was no fault on the part of the company because it had complied with all the requirements of its charter. It was generally understood that that was the law of the whole Dominion except with respect to the province of Quebec, as it is the undoubted law in England ; but their lordships decided that that is also the civil law under the Quebec Civil Code just as it is the law in the other parts of the country. They do not say : We are going to apply to the province of Quebec a law that is in violation of the Quebec Civil Code. On the contrary they say : We construe the law laid down in the Quebec Civil Code to be the same as rules elsewhere. Their lordships may have misconstrued our code, but they have not sought in any way to interfere with our privileges. Without attempting in any way to justify their lordships' judgment, let me put this case to the House. If this is not the law, if this corporation, acting within the rights conferred upon it by its character, is to be liable for tort in the province of Quebec, according to the local law of that province, what becomes of the supremacy of this parliament ? It is a necessary incident of the supremacy of this parliament that it should have the right to confer upon the corporation it creates the right to operate throughout the whole Dominion, and that that right should not be made subject to the action of any local legislature. Otherwise this parliament ceases to be supreme. That seems to me self evident. There is the case and there is nothing more in it, and it seems to me, when we come to consider it, a great tempest in a teapot. I know that in our province we have special privileges. We have an old axiom : Ohaque plaideur a quarante-huit heures pour maudire son juge. Every man who goes before the courts and loses has forty eight hours within which to curse his judge. That is our privilege and we use it, but we ought not to extend that privilege beyond the traditional forty-eight hours.
Motion agreed to.

I notice there is an increase here of $40,000. How is that accounted for ?

There is an apparent increase of $40,000. But I find that last year there was a supplementary estimate of $36,000, and the total expenditure on this service was $202,289. Increased expenditure was caused by the winter mail service to Prince Edward Island, two steamers, the ' Stanley ' and the ' Minto ' being engaged in this service. The effect of the present vote is merely to put into the main estimates a total which was divided last year between the main estimates and the supplementary estimates. I may say also that looking over this matter with the officials of the department I find that, since the two boats were in use for the winter service to Prince Edward Island, this is the least amount for which this service of maintenance and repairs of government steamers can possibly be carried on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: I understand that this ought to contain all that was in the main estimates and in the supplementary estimates last year.
Yes, I agree with my hon. friend. I brought the matter to the attention of the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What repairs are contemplated, and on what vessels ?

The repairs, of course, are an uncertain quantity, the only certain thing being that some repairs will be necessary every season. The principal expense, of course,

is in the maintenance. There are eight of these Dominion steamers, the ' Minto ' and the ' Stanley ' are engaged in the service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. The ' Lansdowne ' has been used on the New Brunswick coast and the Bay of Fundy. The ' Aberdeen ' is in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. The ' Quadra ' is in British Columbia, and the ' Brant,' a small steamer, is in the Prince Edward Island agency. The two boats chartered in place of the ' Druid ' and ' Newfield,' are, one in the Quebec agency and one in Nova Scotia. These are to be replaced next season with two new boats purchased in the old country.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What has become of the ' Druid ' ?
She was condemned and I think sold for $3,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Was there not a boat chartered to take the place of the ' Newfield ' last season ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The other evening, when the estimates of the Minister of Agricultu :e were under discussion, the question came up as to whether the supplementary estimates of last year were included in the column of figures showing the estimates of last year for comparison with the present, and we were told they were so Included. Now, in this item, we have an increase of $40,000, and the minister tells us that the estimates given for last year do not include the supplementary estimates.
There are always the later supplementaries in the following session, which are not included. Except for that the hon. gentleman is correct.

But it is absolutely misleading if we have one minister saying that this includes supplementary estimates and the other saying that in the case of so large an item of $40,000, the supplementary estimates is not included. We want to know whether the figures we have of 1901-2 are correct figures as compared with the estimates of 1902-3, or whether they are incorrect, whether these are correct or whether there are some supplementaries that we do not know about ?	.

The items at the left hand of the vote we have under consideration ought to represent the main estimates for the current year, and also the supplementary estimates, and if they do not in this case it is an error, and I must look into it. But that is what it is intended they should represent. Why they have not done so in this case, I cannot explain, but I will look into it
Then do I understand that these estimates of 1901-2 may in every case not include the supplementary estimates V

They ought to include what I may call the main estimates and the first supplementary estimates for that year, all the votes of last session. My hon. friend knows that there is always a final winding up estimate brought down in the following session. It cannot include that, but it should include the others.
Would the minister tell us now how he purchases these supplies ? Is it by tender, or just giving an order, to merchants in the different ports ?

My information is that prices are asked for by tender for the staple supplies from different parties, and when the prices are ascertained then the goods are ordered. Circulars are sent out to different houses, and prices are asked for in that way for all the staples used on the boats.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will turn up the Auditor General's Report, page 15, he will find the commencement of expenditures for Dominion steamers. The first item I draw to his attention is supplies for steamer ' Lansdowne,' 68 pounds of butter at 35 cents a pound, bought from one of the friends of the government. They purchased $408 worth of supplies, and that is a fair sample of the! charges made. It must have been gilt-edged butter. So it is all through, there is no purchase of supplies by tender. This government, which purchases so vast an amount of supplies, ought to have a warehouse of their own, and draw from that warehouse all they require for the different departments, and buy the goods at wholesale prices. Last night I drew the attention of the House to the Department of the Minister of Agriculture, where we found 168 pounds of putty charged at 8 cents a pound. Turn to the Kingston Penitentiary accounts where everything is bought by tender, and you find putty is bought at $2.25 per 100 pounds. Here you are paying nearly 400 per cent more to one of the government's friends. The late minister, Sir Louis Davies, promised that he would have this matter investigated and have a new state of affairs brought about. But we find the same system continuing, the same men, the same prices charged for supplies all the way through on these steamers. If my hon. friend will turn to the last estimate brought in by the late government in 1895-6, he will find this service was then performed just as effectively as it is now for $166,000, as compared with $243,000 now, an increase of nearly $90,000 in this one item. That shows how the expenditure is creeping up from $37,000,000 to about $57,000,000.

The ' MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. In reply to my hon. friend
I may say that the cost of this service is comparatively about the same as under the previous government. Two boats have been added since the figures that I have spoken of, and no change has been adopted in the system by the present government. Nor am I prepared to admit that one can buy any cheaper, or as cheap probably, in spending a lot of money in advertising for articles wanted on these boats as by asking prices from various well known houses in the different cities where the goods are wanted. I would remind my hon. friend, however, that in making a comparison there are two boats more, last season we had two boats on the route between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I want also to mention to the committee that during the short time at my disposal I find in looking into this matter that the cost of maintenance on these boats has averaged 22 cents per day per man. I hardly think my hon. friend from Deeds (Mr. Taylor) will say that 22 cents per day is an extravagant price for maintenance of officers as well as men employed on the boats. However, in view of the criticisms, I will be pleased, in asking for supplies for the coming year, to look into the matter and see whether or not any saving can be made under the system adopted.

May I ask the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries a question ? In looking at the item in the Auditor General's Report. I see that the vote last year was $196,000, and the expenditure $195,000. That is for Domihion steamers. I am not familiar yet with the way in which accounts are kept, but I suppose these Dominion steamers earn a certain amount of revenue. Where do we find the revenue earned, or is this expenditure over and above any receipts they have in the way of revenue ?
The revenue for the year 1900-1901 was $19,421.68. If my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) will turn to page 4 of the Marine and Fisheries Report, he will find the full account of the revenue.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: If you earned $19,421.68 you expended $196,000.

No, that is no comparison at all. There is only one of these boats in the service that has any revenue at all, and I was very much pleased, in looking into the returns, to see that the revenue was as large as it is on the ' Minto,' which has been engaged in the trade between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, It shows that there is a very good production of commodities on the island and that there is a considerable passenger service. The other boats have no revenue. They are used altogether for maintaining lights and buoys
and other aids to navigation. 1 do not know that this is the place to discuss the question, but after looking into the matter,
I think the hon. gentleman will agree with me that, considering the importance of the transportation question and the lessening of insurance rates, which makes freight charges so high on the St. Lawrence route, it is desirable that more attention should be paid to the subject and that it will be of great advantage to the country that we should improve the aids to navigation, even if it should cost the country a small amount more. My hon. friend will see that the revenue from one boat plying between Prince Edward Island and the mainland was fairly satisfactory.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Mr. Chairman, there is one service for which these steamers are employed which has been overlooked altogether, and that is the prevention of American fishermen from coming within the limits of Dominion waters. These steamers are used around the coast of Prince Edward Island, Cape Breton and Nova Scotia in the spring and fall of the year to prevent American seiners from coming within the three-mile limit. This is one of the most important services that these steamers perform. They have also been used during the last season for repairing and laying down telegraph cables where they were out of order and where new ones were extended, so that to my own knowledge these steamers are kept pretty busy from the opening to the closing of navigation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say in connection with this question, that I think the amount asked for is not excessive. I am pretty well assured that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries will economize in every way to save the people's money. I know that two of these steamers are plying at present between Prince Edward Island and the mainland for the purpose of keeping up communication, for the conveyance of mails, passengers and freight, in accordance with the terms of confederation entered into when Prince Edward Island became a part of the Dominion of Canada. Now, speaking of this increase, we know, as the hon. gentleman has said, that since 1896 the ' Minto ' was constructed in England, brought out here and placed co the service. That boat cost a large amount of money. We have in addition to her the ' Brant,' another boat which is engaged supplying the lighthouses around Prince Edward Island and looking after the lobster fishery. These boats are expensive to maintain each year and we must have an increase in the expenditure. The government surely will not be bound down to a small sum of money, some $40,000 or $50,000 a year, if the service in the maritime provinces is to be fully kept up and maintained. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has gone [DOT] into par-

ticulars in regard to supplies. I have been very exact in that respect and I have taken the precaution to look through the Auditor General's Report. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that supplies purchased for these steamers, in so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, are procured at as low a rate as you could buy the goods in any part of Canada. Whether you get them by tender, or whether you buy them through the captain, or through the agent, you get these supplies, so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, as low as you can obtain similar goods for in any part of this country. I am pleased that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has placed the steamer ' Stanley ' on the western route between Summer-side and Cape Tormentine. That boat is doing good service and this is a very important matter to the people of Prince Edward Island. The mail service has been fairly satisfactory this year, so far as 1 know, and I think there is no doubt that this service if properly managed will be successful. The hon. gentleman has been kind enough, when we represented the matter to him a few days ago, to send down the nautical adviser of the department, Capt. McElhinney to Cape Tormentine and Sum-merside for the purpose of seeing that the work was being properly carried out. While we have had Ministers of Marine and Fisheries from the island, while we have had the late Hon. J. C. Pope, who has gone to his reward, and while we have had Sir. Louis Davies, who has been promoted to the Supreme Court bench, I have not in my experience of twenty-five years found a gentleman more willing to carry out the requests of the people of Prince Edward Island than the hon. minister who is now in charge of the department.

As a general principle we have not been contending that the vote in the main is too large. That has not been our contention, but we have been asking for information to ascertain how this money has been spent There are two ways of spending money and it is a well known fact that one way is usually considered preferable to the other in the event of requiring to spend a large amount of money; one is by purchasing by public tender and the other is by purchasing by private price lists. The hon. member for Prince Edward Island (Mr. Hackett) felt sure that the goods which were bought were bought as cheaply in Prince Edward Island as in any part of Canada. I will not dispute that, because it seems to me on looking over the purchases that there have not been in the main unreasonable prices paid. But, I will give one instance. I will take the village of Westport, not far from Ottawa, where butter was purchased at 35 cents a pound. At what time in the present season has butter been sold, even gilt edged butter, in the city of Montreal for 35 cents a pound ?
The MINISTER OF MARINE- AND FISHERIES. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will find that Westport is a small port down near Yarmouth.
I may tell the hon. gentleman that there was any amount of butter sold in Cape Breton for 35 cents a pound last year.

If these prices prevail down there, all I can say is, that they are much higher than we get for butter in Montreal or Ontario. I speak from knowledge, because I am connected with a butter factory and I know that it was sold from the factory as low as 17i cents or 18 cents, and that was gilt edge butter. However I did-not rise to refer to that particularly. I wish to speak with regard to the system. We had considerable discussion last year and the minister told us that when there were any reasonable purchases to be made they would be made by tender and advertisement, if there was time to do so. I do not say that the bulk of these could be purchased by tender but undoubtedly a fair portion of them could be, and it is the best way to spend the public money. Some of these prices appear to be reasonable enough but some are certainly not. It may be said that when we come to advertise it causes expense. It does if you want to give patronage to the government papers all over the country. But if you pursue a businesslike course the expense of advertising will be comparatively small, and it is the safest thing to do in the public interest.

She was chartered for the season from Geo. E. Boak & Co., Halifax, at $1,500 per month.

speechtext: Was that steamer properly equipped for that service ?
She has been used on the service just as she was hired. There might be the ordinary repairs but nothing of any consequence.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I notice from the report that because the steamer was not properly equipped she was unable to do the work intended for her, and some loss was sustained in consequence, I suppose.
